metadata.title: Poundland could collapse as owners push for insolvency with jobs at risk
metadata.contentSnippet: Poundland could be broken up as owner Gordon Brothers weighs bids for parts of the discount retailer from Wilko, The Range, Poundstretcher and others.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Poundland could collapse as owners push for insolvency with jobs at risk
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Discount retailer Poundland could be broken up as its owners consider offers for parts of the business. Gordon Brothers, which acquired the chain for £1 last year, is currently evaluating multiple bids for the company. A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said: "While Martin Property Group had been identified as the preferred bidder by Poundland’s management team, attention must now turn to other active bids. "As well as interest from buyers for the whole business, the sale process has also surfaced a number of formal and indicative offers for significant viable parts of the business from established retail operators. "These options will now be objectively evaluated, with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland’s people and all relevant stakeholders." A sales process for the business began last month following turnaround efforts that included a series of store closures. Irish real estate firm Martin Property Group was named as the preferred bidder by management earlier this month. Gordon Brothers is therefore assessing a number of other bids, largely from retail rivals, which would involve buying parts of the Poundland business and ultimately see the company enter insolvency. Wilko and The Range owner CDS Superstores, Poundstretcher owner Fortress and TG Jones owner Modella are all among companies interested in buying parts of the retailer. It comes after Trade Union Usdaw shared that it was concerned Gordon Brothers is risking workers' jobs. Usdaw has said that it is worried that Gordon Brothers may decide to pull out and put the company into administration. In a statement put out on Usdaw's website, Bally Auluk – Usdaw national officer said, "With thousands of jobs on the line, it is an absolute disgrace that Gordon Brothers has failed to engage with us to seek a secure future for the business." Usdaw added: "We found it difficult to understand why Poundland was being described as struggling, after the company recently announced they had returned to like-for-like sales growth and staff were being thanked for their ‘amazing efforts’." Poundland currently operates around 600 stores across the UK and employs approximately 12,000 workers. How do you feel about Poundland potentially being broken up? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: Care Network celebrates 40 years after helping thousands across Cambridgeshire
metadata.contentSnippet: A charity is celebrating 40 years of changing lives and strengthening communities across Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Care Network celebrates 40 years after helping thousands across Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A charity is celebrating 40 years of changing lives and strengthening communities across Cambridgeshire. Care Network Cambridgeshire marked the milestone with an event at the William Collyn Community Centre in Girton on Tuesday, October 6, bringing together staff, volunteers, clients, and supporters to reflect on its journey and future plans. Since becoming an established charity in 1986, Care Network has supported thousands of people across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, helping them overcome loneliness, rebuild confidence, access essential services and maintain their independence during challenging times. Sheila Stephenson, founder of Care Network, said: "I am over the moon as to where things have got to." CNC client Alisha (left) and CNC employee Sandra (right) (Image: CNC) One of the most moving moments of the event came when Alisha, a woman in her 20s, shared how Care Network supported her after major brain surgery. Living alone in a new area, she faced isolation, financial hardship, and health struggles. With help from the charity, she accessed financial support, improved her safety at home, and began building connections in her community. Alisha’s story highlighted that care and support are not just for older people—life’s challenges can affect anyone, regardless of age. Care Network began as a small project in Comberton in the 1970s and has since grown into a countywide charity offering services such as Help at Home, RISE, and Community Support. In 2025, it supported 2,479 people, with 94 per cent saying they felt less isolated and 90 per cent reporting improved independence. CNC event with attendees, employees, volunteers and trustees (Image: CNC) Lynda Phillips, chief executive of Care Network Cambridgeshire, said: "One of the things that we are really good at is that we build the support around the individual needs." The charity plans to expand its volunteer network and raise awareness of its services to reach even more people in the years ahead. It remains committed to supporting individuals, strengthening communities, and keeping people at the heart of everything it does.

metadata.title: WATCH: Dramatic footage shows 'deliberate' garage fire in Peterborough
metadata.contentSnippet: Dramatic footage shows the moment a garage in Welland, Peterborough, went up in flames in a fire believed to be deliberate.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: WATCH: Dramatic footage shows 'deliberate' garage fire in Peterborough
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Dramatic footage shows the moment a Cambridgeshire garage went up in flames in a fire believed to be deliberate. Crews from Dogsthorpe and Peterborough Volunteer Fire Brigade were called to Branston Rise, Welland, at 10.26pm on Friday, October 23. Firefighters arrived to find a garage on fire and used breathing apparatus, a hose reel, and a positive pressure ventilation fan to tackle the blaze and clear smoke. They returned to their stations by 11.35pm. The cause of the fire is believed to be deliberate, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service said. Anyone with information should contact police or call Crimestoppers on 0800 555111.

metadata.title: St Ives landmark lit up as 68 babies remembered during Baby Loss Awareness Week
metadata.contentSnippet: A historic landmark was illuminated as part of a heartfelt tribute to bereaved families in St Ives.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Ives landmark lit up as 68 babies remembered during Baby Loss Awareness Week
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A historic landmark was illuminated as part of a heartfelt tribute to bereaved families in St Ives. The town’s medieval bridge and chapel, one of only four of its kind in the UK, was lit up during Baby Loss Awareness Week to raise awareness and offer a space for remembrance. It formed part of the third annual Ribbon Memorial Display, organised by town councillor Laura Thompson and held outside St Ives Methodist Church, who once again supported the memorial by providing use of their fencing. The memorial gave families a space to remember their babies (Image: Baby Loss Awareness Week) Cllr Thompson said: "I wanted to give parents the opportunity to talk about their baby and offer a physical act of remembrance. "I end the week with a roll call of names on the Facebook page, it is so important that parents hear their baby's name spoken aloud." This year, 68 babies were remembered during the week, with nearly 4,000 people viewing the roll call video online. The display was visited by the High Sheriff of Cambridgeshire, who shared his personal connection to the cause. He said: "My wife and I lost a baby very early in a pregnancy, so I feel very connected to this cause. The town’s Bridge and Chapel were illuminated for the awareness week (Image: Baby Loss Awareness Week) "The mayor, Cllr Alex Thompson, and I went to join in on the first day. "By the time we got to the memory wall – only an hour or so after it had opened – over a dozen ribbons had already been tied to the fence, many with loving messages and a child’s name." Eight businesses in St Ives also showed their support by decorating their windows in pink and blue. Cllr Thompson said: "My Facebook page, St Ives Baby Loss Support and Awareness – Cambridgeshire, was viewed over 67,000 times during Baby Loss Week. "These are huge figures and I will keep driving awareness in our town and giving people space to remember."

metadata.title: MP calls for more police officers and funding for schools ahead of UK Budget
metadata.contentSnippet: Rising energy bills and poor access to healthcare are leaving more residents struggling to cope, Ian Sollom, MP for St Neots and Mid-Cambridgeshire, has warned.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MP calls for more police officers and funding for schools ahead of UK Budget
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Rising energy bills and poor access to healthcare are leaving more Huntingdonshire residents struggling to cope, the MP for St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire has warned. Ian Sollom has urged the Chancellor to act urgently on the cost-of-living crisis, health services, schools and policing in the next Budget. He said: "I hear from a wide range of constituents including those who are working, the elderly, disabled and vulnerable people, who tell me they are finding it hard to make ends meet. "They rely on foodbanks and other charities for the basics so they can afford to pay their energy bills and with winter coming, this is very concerning. "I am calling on the Chancellor to help oil-heated households save money on bills by installing heat pumps using funding from the Boiler Upgrade Scheme." Mr Sollom said he had received many requests for help after the rise in energy bills Mr Sollom is also calling for more investment in health services to meet rising demand in the constituency. Mr Sollom said: "I hear weekly from constituents who are unable to get a GP appointment or have to register with a practice miles from their home because there just aren’t the health services available to them in their local area. "This is unacceptable and is only going to get worse as more people move into new developments." Mr Sollom is also calling for more support for Cambridgeshire schools. He said: "Speaking to staff in schools, it is clear that the education funding formula is out of date and not fit for purpose for schools across Cambridgeshire. "Every week I am contacted by parents at their wits’ end who are trying to get their children the support they need as laid out in their Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), but that this support is simply not available to them due to a lack of money." Mr Sollom is calling for fairer funding to schools across Cambridgeshire Mr Sollom added that the funding for Cambridgeshire does not reflect the growth in population and is calling for more police officers on the streets. Mr Sollom is calling for more police officers in Cambridgeshire The next UK Budget, where Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey will outline the state of the economy and the Government's financial plan, is set to take place on October 28. The latest figures available before the Budget showed consumer price inflation at 3.1% in August, up from 2.9% in July and above the Bank of England's 2% target.

metadata.title: MP calls to protect kidney care amid Hinchingbrooke Hospital redevelopment
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdon MP Ben Obese-Jecty is calling for the government to protect dialysis services during a major redevelopment at Hinchingbrooke Hospital.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MP calls to protect kidney care amid Hinchingbrooke Hospital redevelopment
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire MP is calling for the government to protect kidney care during a major hospital redevelopment. Ben Obese-Jecty, MP for Huntingdon, wants a long-term guarantee that dialysis services will continue at Hinchingbrooke Hospital throughout its redevelopment. He visited the renal unit, spoke to staff and patients, and raised concerns about dialysis under the New Hospital Programme. Mr Obese-Jecty said: "Visiting the unit and speaking directly with patients and staff brought home just how vital this service is to our community. "Haemodialysis is physically exhausting and emotionally demanding; local patients should never have to carry the additional anxiety of travelling miles out of our area simply to access life-sustaining treatment." Mr Obese-Jecty has submitted written parliamentary questions to the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), requesting transparent funding commitments and clear confirmation that constituents will not be forced to travel outside Huntingdonshire for regular treatment. He said: "While the rebuild of Hinchingbrooke Hospital is an essential milestone to modernise our health estate and removing reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (RAAC), facility improvements must protect core clinical specialities. "I have taken our community's case to Westminster to secure binding commitments from ministers that renal dialysis will stay right here in Huntingdon for the long term." Patients with end-stage kidney conditions often attend dialysis sessions several times a week. If the service were moved, patients would face lengthy journeys to Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge or Peterborough City Hospital. Hinchingbrooke Hospital was added to the New Hospital Programme in May 2023. North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust invited the public to have their say on site accessibility and navigation; the desired patient and visitor experience, including digital technology and single rooms; and how the hospital can better support community health and wellbeing. The redevelopment programme is designed to address the challenges associated with ageing hospital infrastructure. A new hospital is expected to be delivered on the existing site, due to open by the end of 2032.

metadata.title: Man who bit victim's ear in 'abhorrent' attack pictured for first time

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A man who bit another man's ear during a violent attack has been jailed for more than five years. Douglas Witterick, 45, began attacking the man at a property in Godmanchester, near Huntingdon, at about 3am on April 25. The pair had been talking about people they knew when Witterick flew into a rage, calling the victim a “bully”. The victim went to bed, but Witterick burst into the bedroom and began repeatedly punching him, biting his ear and trying to bite his finger. Witterick, of Park Lane, Godmanchester, left the room but then attacked the victim again, this time in the kitchen, as the latter attempted to leave. He punched and slapped him multiple times, tapped a cannabis grinder on his forehead to intimidate him, kneed him in the thigh and threatened to stab him. Witterick left the property and handed himself in to police at Parkside Police Station in Cambridge on April 28. The victim attended Hinchingbrooke Hospital for treatment for serious but not life-threatening injuries. On Friday (October 23), at Peterborough Magistrates’ Court, acting as a crown court, Witterick, was jailed for five years and four months. He had pleaded guilty to two counts of actual bodily harm at an earlier hearing. He had also breached a suspended sentence following a previous conviction for actual bodily harm and was handed a 12-year restraining order against the victim. DS Karolina Olszewska said: “This was a prolonged and abhorrent attack by Witterick on the victim, which is reflected in the sentence given by the court.” Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: Man stabbed victims in 'completely unprovoked' attack in car park
metadata.contentSnippet: Two men who launched an unprovoked attack in the car park of Co-op in Wisbech Lane, Littleport.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Man stabbed victims in 'completely unprovoked' attack in car park
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two men who launched an unprovoked attack outside a shop in Cambridgeshire have been sentenced. Joshua Davidson and Kai O’Donnell attacked two men in the car park of the Co-op, in Wisbech Lane, Littleport on May 18. The victims, aged 29 and 58, were leaving the store at around 7.50pm when they were punched. Davidson then pulled out a weapon and began slashing at the them. When the younger man fell to the ground, the pair continued the attack. The group then moved to Friars Lane, where the violence continued until a member of the public intervened and called police. Officers located the victims at their nearby home and they were taken to hospital, where they were treated for multiple serious but not life-threatening stab wounds. Armed officers later arrested Davidson and O’Donnell in Tilling Way. At Peterborough Crown Court yesterday (26 October), Davidson, 21, of no fixed address, was sentenced to five years in prison. He pleaded guilty to two counts of wounding with intent and possession of a bladed article in a public place. O’Donnell, 21, of Tilling Way, Littleport, pleaded guilty to affray and was sentenced to 19 months in prison, suspended for two years. He must also carry out 100 hours of unpaid work. Detective Constable Charmaine Wood, who investigated, said: "This was a completely unprovoked attack on two men. "Davidson’s decision to carry and use a weapon turned an already violent incident into one which could have had even more serious consequences. "There is no place for this kind of violence in our communities, and I hope these sentences provide some reassurance that those responsible have been held to account." metadata.title: Hunts nursery closes with immediate effect after 'safeguarding incident'
metadata.contentSnippet: The Anchor Nursery and Pre-School in King's Ripton, Huntingdonshire, has closed for six weeks with immediate effect after its registration was suspended.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts nursery closes with immediate effect after 'safeguarding incident'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire nursery has closed with immediate effect after its registration was suspended. It is understood The Anchor Nursery and Pre-School in King's Ripton, near Huntingdon, shut on Friday (October 23) after the suspension by Ofsted. Golden Apples Nurseries, which operates the site, has since confirmed a "safeguarding incident" occurred at the site on October 21. A spokesperson said: "Immediate action was taken in line with safeguarding procedures, and we continue to work closely with the relevant authorities. "The safety and wellbeing of every child in our care remains our highest priority." Although the education watchdog said it does not comment on individual providers, its guidance on suspension is clear. Ofsted will suspend a provider's registration if it "believes a child or children may be at risk of harm". However, suspension is not a final finding of guilt or fault but an interim measure designed to safeguard children. The minimum suspension period for a childcare provider's registration is six weeks, which allows Ofsted time to investigate concerns. Cambridgeshire County Council said it was aware of the suspension and confirmed it had resulted in "the immediate closure of the setting". A spokesperson for the local authority said: "We understand this must be unsettling for affected families. "A member of our Early Years Team has attended the nursery to support the management of the situation and provide parents and carers with further information about support available. "We have also issued letters to parents and carers detailing where they can find support with alternative childcare places." The Anchor Nursery and Pre-School was first thrust into the spotlight when it notified Ofsted of a "serious incident" in June 2024. By notifying the watchdog, the nursery met its legal responsibility under the 'statutory framework for the early years foundation stage'. However, after a regulatory telephone call, Ofsted "found the provider was not meeting one of the requirements". This related to safeguarding policies and procedures not being implemented in line with the guidance and procedures of the relevant local safeguarding partners. At the time, Ofsted confirmed the nursery took "immediate action to strengthen their safeguarding policies and procedures". Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: What will Budget mean for pensioners as State Pension set to hit £13,036?
metadata.contentSnippet: What will Budget mean for pensioners as State Pension set to hit £13,036 as Chancellor John Healey to announce a major change.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: What will Budget mean for pensioners as State Pension set to hit £13,036?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of pensioners are waiting to see whether Chancellor John Healey will announce a major change to the tax-free personal allowance in the Budget 2026. The Government is expected to set out how it will protect people whose only income is the State Pension from paying Income Tax, after next April’s increase is set to push the full new State Pension above the existing £12,570 personal allowance. According to some reports, ministers are considering raising the tax-free threshold for low-income pensioners to £13,036, matching the projected annual value of the full new State Pension from April 2027. This could shield almost one million pensioners from Income Tax and cost around £200million a year by the end of the decade. However, the reported plan would not mean every pensioner becomes exempt from tax. People with private pensions, savings income or other sources of taxable income could still face an Income Tax bill. The full new State Pension is on course to increase by 3.9% from April 2027 under the triple lock. This would take the weekly payment from £241.30 to £250.70, an annual increase of around £489, bringing the yearly total to approximately £13,036. The increase reflects earnings growth, which is one of three measures used to determine the annual State Pension rise. Under the triple lock, payments increase each April by whichever is highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%. The projected increase would take the full new State Pension above the current £12,570 Income Tax personal allowance for the first time. The personal allowance is the amount someone can earn in a tax year before they start paying Income Tax. Without a change to the rules, pensioners whose only income is the full new State Pension could technically have a small amount of income above the standard tax-free threshold. The Government has previously promised that people whose only income is the State Pension will be protected from paying Income Tax, with further details expected in the Budget. The Times reports that ministers intend to achieve this by increasing the personal allowance for low-income pensioners to £13,036. If introduced as reported, the measure could mean almost one million pensioners avoid paying Income Tax on their State Pension. The proposed threshold would also rise in line with increases to the State Pension during the current Parliament, according to the newspaper. However, the details of how eligibility would work have not yet been confirmed. Steve Webb, a partner at pension consultants LCP, warned that the policy could create difficulties if the higher allowance is restricted to people on low incomes. He said: “The gap between the new state pension and the tax threshold is set to grow every year, which will make the policy hard to switch off. “But if it continues, the cost will grow and grow. And if the extra allowance is available only to those on a low income, there could be a growing ‘cliff edge’ problem where those with very small amounts of private income lose the whole allowance and end up worse off than those with nothing.” The concern is that someone with a small private pension could lose access to the additional allowance and end up paying more tax than someone whose only income is the State Pension. Pensioners receiving the basic State Pension under the old system will also see their payments increase next April. Under the projected 3.9% rise, the full basic State Pension would increase from £184.90 to £192.10 a week. That would amount to around £9,989 a year, leaving it below the existing £12,570 personal allowance. However, many people who reached State Pension age under the old system receive additional payments on top of the basic pension. These can include additional State Pension entitlements, such as the State Earnings-Related Pension Scheme (SERPS), meaning their total income may be higher. The amount someone receives depends on their National Insurance record and individual circumstances. People with gaps in their contributions may receive less than the full new State Pension. The tax proposal comes as the Government has also announced plans to adjust how the triple lock operates from April 2030. Under the proposals outlined by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the State Pension would continue to rise by at least inflation or 2.5%, while still tracking average earnings over time. The Government says the overhaul would help fund a new National Care Service in England. Any change to the triple lock could have implications for pensioners' future income, particularly as the State Pension continues to rise alongside wages and inflation. Recommended reading: The Budget is also expected to settle questions about whether the Government will change the amount people can withdraw from their private pensions tax-free. There had been speculation that ministers were considering cutting the maximum tax-free lump sum from £268,275 to £100,000. People can normally withdraw up to 25% of their pension pot tax-free, subject to the relevant limits and protections. The normal minimum pension age is 55, rising to 57 from April 2028 for most people.

metadata.title: Nine Cambs council workers sacked in one year after disciplinary hearings
metadata.contentSnippet: Nine Cambridgeshire County Council employees were sacked last year following disciplinary hearings, data has revealed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Nine Cambs council workers sacked in one year after disciplinary hearings
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nine county council employees were sacked last year following disciplinary hearings, data has revealed. A Freedom of Information Act request to Cambridgeshire County Council found that there were a total of 57 disciplinary hearings over the last three years. In the 2024/25 financial year, there were 22 disciplinary hearings with nine resulting in the employee’s contract being terminated. This was higher than the year before, 2023/24, when there were just seven hearings and less than five dismissals. To protect privacy, exact figures for numbers under five have not been provided. In 2025/26, there were 28 disciplinary hearings but less than five of these resulted in the employee being sacked. The most common reasons for disciplinary action were breach of policy and procedure and safeguarding, with 13 cases of each across the three years. This was followed by inappropriate communication or behaviour, with 11 cases, and health and safety with ten cases. There were less than five cases each of hearings for absence, bullying, harassment or discrimination, fraud, financial or theft, gross misconduct and negligence. A spokesperson for Cambridgeshire County Council said they pride themselves “on being a compassionate and inclusive employer”. They said: “That does not mean that we avoid dealing with inappropriate or unacceptable conduct by our employees – the council is equally committed to achieving high standards across our workforce of more than 4,500 people. “Disciplinary hearings, where necessary, occur following robust and fair investigation processes. “Importantly, disciplinary processes do not and should not always result in the dismissal of employees. “Other sanctions, such as warnings, are available to the council and are applied where appropriate. “The FOI request did not ask for details of these outcomes, it only asked about dismissals.” In 2025, a council worker was sacked after the county council was scammed out of more than £90,000 in a bank mandate fraud. A fraudster had submitted falsified documents to change the bank details of a contracted home-to-school transport supplier and four payments totalling £93,000 were sent to the fraudster’s account. By the time it was discovered, Cambridgeshire Police found that the “suspected fraudster had left the country,” according to council documents. The officer in charge of verifying changes of bank details said they called the supplier and spoke to the owner to verify the change, but the council found they had not done this. They were dismissed for gross misconduct after falsifying a document to say they had conducted these checks, which the council said could have prevented the fraud.

metadata.title: Royal Mail reveals new stamps to mark Armistice Day and honour Armed Forces
metadata.contentSnippet: Royal Mail will issue six Remembrance stamps on November 11, marking 110 years since the Battle of the Somme.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Royal Mail reveals new stamps to mark Armistice Day and honour Armed Forces
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new set of stamps honouring the service of the nation’s armed forces has been revealed. Royal Mail will release six stamps on Armistice Day, November 11, marking 110 years since the Battle of the Somme, which began on July 1, 1916, and became one of the defining battles of the First World War. The stamps feature specially commissioned artworks by British artist Matthew Cook, who has served as a reservist in the Parachute Regiment and The Rifles and was deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan. David Gold of Royal Mail, said: "Remembrance holds a profound place in our national life. "Through these stamps, we pay tribute to the service and sacrifice of those who have served our country through two world wars and many other conflicts. Six new stamps have been released. (Image: Royal Mail/Press Association) "Matthew Cook’s poignant artworks provide a fitting and powerful way to reflect on the sacrifices made by so many courageous men and women across the generations." Cook said: “Remembrance has a very special place in my life, having served as a reservist in the Parachute Regiment and The Rifles and been deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan. “I was delighted to be asked to illustrate these stamps and to take on the challenge of such a sensitive and significant subject. “It is always a privilege to illustrate stamps for Royal Mail, and this project felt particularly special.” If stamps are placed in the wrong place, it could mean the parcel or letter will be delayed because Royal Mail’s sorting machines are programmed to scan that specific area. The automatic machines might also mark the item as having no postage paid, which could mean the person receiving the item will have to pay a fee for it. The recipient can visit the sorting office and look at the envelope but if they do not know who the parcel is from or do not want to pay the fee, the item will be kept for 18 days before it is returned to the sender or destroyed. There are a few other rules that Royal Mail says people should follow to avoid any delays or fees for their items. The stamp should also be placed completely flat and visible with the Queen or King’s head facing the right way up. The area around the stamp must also be kept clear, as Royal Mail uses the space for tracking codes and digital postmarks. Writing over the stamp will make it difficult for Royal Mail machines to read the tracking code. Royal Mail says: "The days of licking stamps are over. "Just peel your stamp and stick it in the top right-hand corner of your letter. "You’ll need your stamp to be clearly visible, not bent over an edge and on the same face of your parcel as the address. "Many stamps contain barcodes to assist in tracking, so it’s important that the stamp is flat and easy to scan."

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire fire chiefs urge families to attend organised fireworks displays
metadata.contentSnippet: Fire chiefs in Cambridgeshire are urging families to attend organised displays.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire fire chiefs urge families to attend organised fireworks displays
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Fire chiefs in Cambridgeshire are urging families to attend organised displays. With firework season approaching and schools breaking up for half-term, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service is reminding the public of the dangers posed by home fireworks and bonfires. Station Commander Scott Fretwell, community risk manager, said: "Bonfire Night is a very popular fixture in the calendar and can be plenty of fun for all of the family to enjoy. "There are, however, potential hazards to avoid, to help keep you and your family safe. "We urge anyone wanting to enjoy fireworks to attend an organised fireworks display rather than hosting your own. "There are many across the county that people can enjoy safely, which can be found on an interactive map on our website." While organised events are safest, the fire service acknowledges that many people will still choose to hold celebrations at home. Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service is urging residents to stay safe and attend an organised fireworks display (Image: Supplied) Scott said: "While most people enjoy fireworks responsibly, in the wrong hands they can cause injury and damage to property. "Fireworks are explosives and as such should be treated with respect and only used in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions and the firework safety code. "Lighting a bonfire in a garden presents significant risks to residents if they get out of hand. "Not only this, but the smoke can also aggravate neighbours with respiratory problems. "They can also get out of control very quickly, causing damage to property and sometimes serious injury." The fire service advises only buying fireworks with a CE mark, lighting them at arm’s length with a taper, and never returning to a lit firework. They also warn against giving sparklers to children under five and recommend keeping pets indoors throughout the evening. For those who do decide to light a bonfire, the service urges residents to build it well clear of buildings and fences, avoid burning hazardous items, and never leave it unattended.

metadata.title: 40,000 sign petition to save 'essential' BBC show as its 'rested' after 27 years
metadata.contentSnippet: More than 40,000 people have signed a petition to save DIY SOS after the BBC said the show will be rested in 2027 amid ongoing cost cuts.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 40,000 sign petition to save 'essential' BBC show as its 'rested' after 27 years
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than 40,000 people have signed a petition to save the BBC’s long-running home renovation series DIY SOS. The show, which first aired in 1999 and is currently fronted by Nick Knowles, is set to be “rested” in 2027 as part of the broadcaster’s latest round of cost-cutting measures. DIY SOS has earned a loyal following by transforming the homes of families facing severe illness, disability, bereavement, or building disasters, with the help of volunteers and tradespeople from local communities. The BBC’s decision has prompted a wave of public backlash. A Change.org petition calling for the show to be saved has already surpassed 40,400 signatures. The petition states: "In 2025, I had the extraordinary privilege of contributing to a show on the BBC that has made a profound impact on the lives of countless individuals. "This wasn't just another reality TV series; it was a beacon of hope for those struggling in difficult circumstances. "The show brought together a community of tradespeople who volunteered their time, skills, and resources to make miraculous transformations in people's living situations, changing lives for the better. "This program showcased raw and heartfelt stories of real people, grappling with the hardships of everyday life. "It highlighted the power of compassion and community, bringing viewers not just entertainment, but also a myriad of invaluable life lessons. "For the many families it has helped, the show has been nothing less than life-changing, offering them a chance at a fresh start and an improved future. "Unfortunately, there are discussions underway about cancelling this invaluable show. "Ending it means turning away from those in need and ignoring the good it brings. "At a time when reality often feels overwhelmingly challenging, this show stands as a reminder to all of us of the potential we have to make a difference in our communities. "We urge the BBC to reconsider any plans to cancel this essential program. "By preserving it, we continue to foster a spirit of generosity, empathy, and community support that the show so beautifully encapsulates. "Let us keep telling these important stories and making a tangible difference in people's lives." The BBC has confirmed that DIY SOS will be rested after its current series concludes. The corporation insists the programme has not been permanently cancelled, with a new spin-off show revisiting families and renovation projects from its history set to take its place. A BBC spokesperson said: "In light of the BBC’s savings challenges we have taken the decision to rest DIY SOS in 2027 and commission a new spin-off show instead from producers South Shore. "DIY SOS Rebuilt My Life will revisit successes from the show’s past and expand the brand on the BBC in a more cost-effective way next year." The BBC has also rested the annual DIY SOS Children In Need special, which typically involves a large-scale charitable project supporting young people. These decisions form part of wider efforts to save £500 million over the next three years, which have already resulted in the cancellation of other popular programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, and Live At The Apollo. DIY SOS presenter Nick Knowles said he was "disappointed" by the decision but acknowledged the financial pressures facing the broadcaster. Knowles said: "You may have already seen the news that DIY SOS is being put on 'pause.' "Of course, I’m disappointed not to be filming the show next year or again in the same format we know and love. "But I do understand there’s no endless pot of money at the BBC and sometimes they have to make difficult decisions. "For 26 years it’s been an honour and a privilege to be part of DIY SOS and I’ve loved nothing more than making it. "What I always come back to is that it’s the people who are the beating heart of SOS. "It really is the best of Britain and we need to see more of it on telly." He also thanked the families, volunteers, production team, and viewers who have supported the show over the years. Knowles continued: "To the volunteers, production team, purple shirts, commissioners and everyone watching at home, we couldn’t have done this without you. "And to everyone who hasn’t seen the series yet, give it a watch. "I promise your heart will be warmed." Are you upset by the BBC's decision to "rest" DIY SOS in 2027? Let us know in the poll above or in the comments below.

metadata.title: Asda recalls 3 major fashion items due to safety concerns for shoppers
metadata.contentSnippet: Asda is recalling three styles of handbags after they were found to contain excessive levels of phthalates.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Asda recalls 3 major fashion items due to safety concerns for shoppers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Asda has issued an urgent product recall over safety concerns. The supermarket chain is recalling three styles of handbags after they were found to contain excessive levels of phthalates. These are chemical compounds used to soften plastics, which can pose health risks. It was found the bags present a potential health risk because they contain excessive levels of phthalates (Image: Kennedy News & Media) A spokesperson for Asda said: "At the time of shipment, this product successfully passed all required tests. "However, subsequent testing has identified that it may contain phthalates at levels exceeding the permitted regulatory limit. "Certain phthalates, including Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP), are subject to regulatory restrictions because prolonged exposure above specified limits may pose potential health risks and possibly cause damage to the reproductive system. "While no safety incidents have been reported, we're taking this action to ensure compliance with applicable regulations and to maintain our commitment to consumer safety. "The product doesn't meet the requirements of the REACH Regulations. "If you've purchased this bag, please bring it back to your nearest store where you will be given a full refund. "You do not need your receipt. "We're very sorry for any inconvenience caused. "If you'd like any further information, please contact Asda Customer Relations – 0330 053 0111." The recall applies to three products: The bags were sold for between £8 and £12.50. Customers are advised to return the items to their nearest Asda store for a full refund. If there is a problem with a food product that means it should not be sold, it may be 'withdrawn' from shelves or 'recalled' when customers are asked to return it. The Food Standards Agency issues allergy alerts when foods have to be withdrawn or recalled because of missing or incorrect allergy labelling, or if there is any other food allergy risk. Have you ever had to return an item due to a product recall? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: Senior doctors in England to strike for 2 days - what does it mean for patients?
metadata.contentSnippet: The British Medical Association has announced a two-day strike action for November for senior doctors in England

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Senior doctors in England to strike for 2 days - what does it mean for patients?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Senior doctors in England are to stage a two-day strike next month in a dispute over pay and pensions. The walkout will begin on Wednesday, November 25 at 6.59am, with consultants providing emergency cover only. The strike follows a British Medical Association (BMA) ballot in which 76% of participating consultants voted in favour of industrial action. Talks had taken place with the government over the past month. Consultants don’t want to strike, but after 18 months without formal negotiations, they cannot wait any longer. These strikes are planned to take place on 25 and 26 November, with Christmas Day levels of cover provided. There is still time for the Government to make progress. https://t.co/tco6pyInD8 — The BMA (@TheBMA) October 26, 2026 In a statement, the BMA said: "Our intended industrial action will take the form of ‘Christmas Day’ cover as in previous industrial action. "Consultants provide safe emergency and immediately life-saving care on Christmas day and out of hours 365 days a year, so no patients will be harmed but the Government will hear our message loud and clear. "If the Government chooses to act, by formally negotiating with us with a mandate that can lead to a credible offer across our range of demands, then industrial action can and will be stood down." Consultants – the most senior doctors in the NHS – were given a 3.5% pay increase this year. Basic pay for consultants starts at £113,500 with the most experienced paid £150,500. However, they can earn thousands of pounds in extra payments, which means average earnings are more than £150,000 a year. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government had been in "constructive discussions" with the BMA, so it was "disappointing" that the strike dates had been announced. She said taking strike action would be "irresponsible" and "place the health service under even greater pressure". In previous strike actions by resident doctors, patients have been warned that procedures could be cancelled, but urgent appointments should continue as normal. Patients will be contacted if their planned procedures cannot go ahead. NHS England has said in previous strike actions that hospitals should only cancel non-urgent care, such as hip and knee operations, in exceptional circumstances.

metadata.title: Co-op becomes first UK retailer to get viral sweet treat in 1,600 stores
metadata.contentSnippet: Co-op will be launching its own version of the viral Dot Cake in stores for a limited period of six weeks

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Co-op becomes first UK retailer to get viral sweet treat in 1,600 stores
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Co-op has claimed it has become the first retailer to bring a viral sweet treat to UK stores. Dot Cakes have amassed attention on platforms like TikTok recently, after a video from a New York bakery showing one off gained traction. The dessert is usually a small cake served in a cup, pot or ramekin, layered with sponge and buttercream, then topped with a thick layer of tiny round sprinkles. The cakes have since attracted millions of fans globally online, with many creating their own DIY versions at home. Co-op will now stock its own version in more than 1,600 stores across the UK for a limited period of six weeks. A spokesperson for Co-op said: "Staying true to the original flavours social media users love, Co-op’s Raspberry & Vanilla Dot Cake (166g, £2.50) combines vanilla flavour sponge, layered with raspberry jam and vanilla flavour frosting, topped with multi-coloured sugar decorations. "Chocolate lovers can also get their hands on the retailer’s Chocolate & Salted Caramel Dot Cake (177g, £2.50), featuring fluffy chocolate flavour sponge, layered with salted caramel and chocolate caramel flavour frosting, finished with white and milk chocolate crispy balls." Kevin Sargent, senior product development manager for cake at Co-op, said: "We're excited to be hot on the heels of one of this year's biggest food trends by being the first retailer to bring them to shops across the UK. The Dot Cakes come in two flavours in Raspberry & Vanilla and Chocolate & Salted Caramel (Image: Co-op) "They tap into everything people love right now – aesthetically pleasing, nostalgic treats that are as fun to eat as they are to share online. "With two delicious flavour combinations and that signature crunchy topping, we're making it easier for shoppers across the country to get their hands on the viral treat and see what all the fuss is about!" Back in September, Co-op brought back a popular crisp flavour after a three-year absence. The retailer originally launched Roast Potato Crisps in 2019, and they quickly gained a loyal following thanks to their "surprisingly bold taste". Combining sea salt, garlic, rosemary and black pepper, the crisps are designed to "capture the taste of a classic Christmas roast potato". However, they disappeared from Co-op shelves in 2023, prompting shoppers to call for their return. The flavour has now made a comeback as Irresistible Ultimate Roast Potato Crinkle Cut Crisps (150g), one of three flavours included in Co-op's new Christmas range for 2026. Recommended reading: Crisps, snacks and nuts development manager at Co-op, Natalie Dawe, said: "Our crisps have developed something of a cult following over the years, with our customers regularly championing their favourites. "This year, we're delighted to bring back our Roast Potato Crisps and what I love about them is that the flavour always sparks discussion… it’s much more than meets the eye. "Combining salt, garlic, rosemary and black pepper to recreate the taste of perfectly seasoned roasties." Will you be looking to get a Dot Cake in Co-op stores? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: We braved the UK's longest scare maze as Horror Mania returns to Cambridgeshire
metadata.contentSnippet: Horror Mania returns to Cambridgeshire, with its claimed longest continuous UK scare maze, 100 plus actors and Halloween frights galore/

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We braved the UK's longest scare maze as Horror Mania returns to Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Blood-curdling screams filled the air as we pulled up at the Horror Mania event in Cambridgeshire on Sunday evening, as hundreds of people queued for a night of fright. Staged at Skylark Garden Centre in Wimblington, the event boasts it is the longest continuous scare maze in the UK. The popular horror attraction was cancelled earlier this year after its previous venue, Hinchingbrooke House in Huntingdon, decided to no longer host it. Robert Gough, director of Horror Mania, said they had been worried the event, which attracts thousands of horror fans, would not come back following the cancellation as it needed the right venue to continue. There are plenty of moments to get the adrenaline pumping in the Horror Mania maze - the longest one in the UK. (Image: Sarah Cliss/Horror Mania) Happily, Robert and his team have found that at Skylark. The immersive scare maze has taken two months to build, and the effort was certainly worthwhile, with a variety of marquees with various horror themes delivering plenty of jumps, screams and frights guaranteed to get the adrenaline pumping, and the imagination racing. With more than 100 actors bringing the horror to life, the event is a whole lot of fun for those brave enough to venture into the maze. Loud music, flashing strobe lights, fog and lots of twists and turns with unexpected jumps around every corner; it is certainly not for the faint-hearted. Even knowing it is just a laugh, and that you are not really being confronted by an Egyptian mummy, or a zombie Taylor Swift, the scares are still realistic enough to put your nerves on edge. There were a few visitors nervous about entering some of the marquees, most notably the Clown City one, which was littered with terrifying clowns - as if they were not already scary enough for some people. The Stinkyface World was particularly gut-wrenching, mainly because it smelled just like poo - not for those with a delicate stomach. I won't go into too much detail on what you might find, as I don't want to spoil the surprise/horror/shock for visitors. But suffice to say if you love a bit of horror and are looking for a night of fun this Halloween, then Horror Mania at Skylark is the place to be. Tickets are on sale - although there may be limited availability for some time slots - from £29.95 to £52.95 per person. There are no age restrictions; however, Horror Mania is frightening and is not really suitable for children under 16. Under-16s must be accompanied by an adult.

metadata.title: Fire service update on cause of fire at proposed asylum seeker site
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service has given a major update about the cause of a fire at proposed asylum seeker site Roman Court in Leverington.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Fire service update on cause of fire at proposed asylum seeker site
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A fire service has given a major update about the cause of a fire at a proposed asylum seeker site in Cambridgeshire. Firefighters were called to the blaze at Roman Court, Leverington, near Wisbech, at 7.26pm on Wednesday (October 21). Firefighters from Wisbech, March and Dogsthorpe attended, alongside the turntable ladder from Stanground and crews from Outwell and West Walton in Norfolk. They found a blaze in a single-storey building which was unoccupied and worked to stop the fire spreading. No injuries were reported but the building has been "severely damaged", police said. Firefighters were called to Roman Court in Leverington (Image: Supplied) Crews left the scene at about 10.30pm after extinguishing the fire. Firefighters inspected the scene the following morning to check it was safe and that there had been no further spread or hot spots. Police said on Thursday, October 22, that they were treating the fire as arson and investigating it. In an update on October 23, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service confirmed that a "complex fire investigation" had been carried out. However, due to the significant damage to the building and firefighting operations, a precise cause could not be determined. Roman Court has been at the centre of an asylum row since the government announced plans to house 26 mothers and babies at the site. The site has attracted protests over its potential use as asylum seeker accommodation (Image: Supplied/Chris Tirrell) In September, Fenland District Council revealed it had been told by the Home Office the site could "provide 26 bed spaces for mothers and babies". The proposal is part of a national plan to move asylum seekers from hotels into longer-term accommodation. A Home Office spokesperson said: "Any form of criminal damage is completely unacceptable. "The safety of local communities will always be our highest priority, and the police have our full support in their investigation." The department declined to comment on Roman Court, citing its longstanding policy of not discussing individual accommodation sites.

metadata.title: WATCH: Disqualified driver who fled from officers sniffed out by police dog
metadata.contentSnippet: A disqualified driver who fled from officers at Brampton Hut Services and was sniffed out by a police dog has been handed a suspended prison sentence.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: WATCH: Disqualified driver who fled from officers sniffed out by police dog
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A disqualified driver who fled from officers and was sniffed out by a police dog has been handed a suspended prison sentence and a driving ban. Fabio Sanches-Kuiper, 19, of Dovecote Avenue, Great Cambourne, was spotted by officers getting into a BMW at Brampton Hut Services at 11.20pm on September 23. Police had intelligence that he was driving again despite court-imposed bans. Road Policing Unit officers deployed a stinger on the A141, but Sanches-Kuiper refused to stop, drove towards Brampton, then abandoned the BMW and fled into nearby bushes. He was arrested with the help of police dog Ghost. At Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on Monday, October 19, Sanches-Kuiper admitted two counts of driving without insurance, two counts of driving while disqualified and failing to stop. He was jailed for 20 weeks, suspended for 18 months, and given a six-month curfew from 11pm to 6am. He was also banned from driving for four years. PC Colin Dyer, of the Road Policing Unit, said: "Despite being disqualified from driving and previously serving a prison sentence for the offence, Sanches-Kuiper made the decision to get behind the wheel yet again and on one occasion attempted to evade officers. “Driving bans are imposed to protect the public and reduce the risk posed by dangerous drivers. "His repeated offending showed a complete disregard for those restrictions.”

metadata.title: New eight-home development in Warboys approved despite resident objections
metadata.contentSnippet: Plans for eight homes in Warboys have been approved despite objections from residents and the parish council.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New eight-home development in Warboys approved despite resident objections
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans for a new eight-home development in Warboys have been approved despite objections from residents and the parish council. The proposal, from applicants Mr and Mrs Robinson, involves constructing eight detached homes on land between Heath Farm and Heath Pond, north of Heath Road in Warboys. The land is currently classed as agricultural. Plans include three three-bedroom and five four-bedroom homes, 16 parking spaces, landscaping and a footpath linking the site to the village. It was granted Permission in Principle in July 2025 for between four and nine homes, establishing that the site could be developed for housing. The plans include three-bedroom and four-bedroom homes, 16 parking spaces and landscaping (Image: Huntingdonshire Planning Portal) Despite the formal submission of these plans, the proposal has faced objections from Warboys Parish Council and residents. The parish council objected because the site is located near a former sheep dip, raising concerns over land contamination and risk to human health and the environment. The council added: "In addition, concerns are raised regarding highway safety, as the proposed access is located close to the junction with the A141, a heavily trafficked route, which is considered likely to result in a substandard and potentially hazardous access arrangement." Five residents lodged complaints, with concerns ranging from highway safety due to the proximity of the site to the A141 junction, to the loss of agricultural land and countryside. Residents also fear the homes will put more pressure on the local GP surgery and primary school. However, planning officers have recommended the approval of the application, arguing that the benefits of the development outweigh these concerns. They pointed out that the district has only a 3.68-year supply of housing land, against the required five-year supply, indicating an unmet housing need. The development is subject to several planning conditions, comprising requirements for landscaping, drainage measures, noise mitigation, cycle storage, archaeological investigation, and off-site highway improvements.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A popular Christmas light trail is set to return, promising festive magic and sparkling displays for visitors of all ages. Wimpole Estate will once again transform its historic gardens into an illuminated winter wonderland from November 20, 2026, to January 3, 2027. Created by internationally acclaimed producers, the trail features immersive soundscapes and dazzling light installations set to seasonal music. James Dakin, director of live experiences at RG Live, said: "With just under one month to go until we officially open our doors, Christmas at Wimpole promises an evening of breath-taking light installations and festive discovery, with unexpected surprises woven throughout, creating memories that go well beyond a typical festive night." Christmas at Wimpole Estate returns from November 20, 2026, to January 3, 2027, with a dazzling light trail, festive food and new Ribbon Tunnel. (Image: Oliver Dixon) Visitors will begin their journey under a canopy of twinkling lights before passing through the Christmas Cathedral and the glowing Fire Garden. The trail also includes illuminated trees and a new interactive Ribbon Tunnel for 2026. Along the route, guests can enjoy festive food and drink, from burgers and hot dogs to cheese wheels and children's meals. All stalls offer meat-free and gluten-free options to ensure everyone can join in the festivities. A spokesperson for the event said: "Christmas at Wimpole 2026 promises an evening of light, wonder and festive joy, with plenty of moments to pause, look up, and capture festive photos along the route." Organisers recommend booking early, as the event operates with limited capacity and timed entry slots. Tickets for adults start at £18 off-peak, rising to £26 during peak times, while children's tickets range from £13 to £19.50. All prices include a £1 booking fee, and infants under two years old can attend free of charge. Additional charges apply for fairground rides. The illuminated trail is designed for all ages and aims to create lasting memories during the festive season. Wimpole Estate, located in Royston, Cambridgeshire, is a National Trust property known for its grand house, gardens, and parkland. Visitors are encouraged to dress warmly and arrive on time to enjoy the full experience as the estate lights up in celebration of Christmas.

metadata.title: 8 fantastic bakeries in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once
metadata.contentSnippet: From artisan sourdough specialists and to French pâtisseries, here are eight bakeries in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 8 fantastic bakeries in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From artisan sourdough specialists and to French pâtisseries, Cambridgeshire is packed with fantastic bakeries producing exceptional baked goods. These eight locations have built loyal followings, thanks to their quality breads, pastries, cakes and customer service and are a must visit. If you're craving authentic French baking without crossing the Channel, Maison Clément Bakery & Patisserie is one of the county's stand-out destinations. Opened in 2017, the business has become renowned for its buttery croissants, pain au chocolat and delicate pâtisserie creations. Customers regularly praise the bakery's authenticity, quality ingredients and traditional techniques. Perhaps unsurprisingly, this bakery boasts a rating of 4.6 stars out of 5 on Google based off more than 570 reviews. Nestled on St Mary's Street, Grain Culture Bake Shop has transformed itself from a small artisan operation into one of Cambridgeshire's most celebrated bakeries. The business is particularly known for its exceptional sourdough loaves, flaky pastries and carefully sourced produce. Customers frequently praise the welcoming atmosphere alongside the bakery's excellent coffee and inventive range of baked goods. It has a rating of 4.8 stars out of 5 on Google based off more than 240 reviews. A relatively small bakery with an enormous reputation, Welch Bakes has become one of St Neots' most loved independent businesses. Visitors regularly highlight its outstanding sourdough bread, brownies, blondies and artisan pastries. Many customers also praise the friendly owners and welcoming service. Welch Bakes has an impressive rating of 5 stars out of 5 on Google based off more than 90 reviews. Situated in the heart of St Ives, Tom's Cakes has built an excellent reputation for its vast array of cakes, traybakes, pastries and brownies. The bakery and café is frequently praised by customers for both the quality and variety of its offerings. Whether you're after a classic Victoria sponge, a rich brownie or a fresh pastry, there's something for everyone. It boasts a rating of 4.6 stars out of 5 on Google based off more than 270 reviews. In an era increasingly dominated by chain stores, Peter's Traditional Bakery remains proudly old-school. Fresh bread, savoury pastries, sausage rolls, cakes and pies line the shelves each day, attracting loyal customers from across Peterborough. Reviews regularly mention the bakery's traditional charm, reasonable prices and welcoming staff. This bakery has a rating of 4.8 stars out of 5 on Google based off 280 reviews. A Cambridge institution since 1920, Fitzbillies is arguably the county's most famous bakery. It is best known for its legendary Chelsea buns, which continue to draw visitors from across the country. Beyond the signature bake, customers praise the bakery's range of breads, pastries and café offerings. Combining history, quality and a unique place in Cambridge's food scene, it remains an essential stop for anyone exploring the city. It has a rating of 4.1 stars out of 5 on Google based off more than 2,800 reviews. With roots stretching back more than a century, Dorringtons has built a loyal customer base through dependable quality and traditional baking expertise. Customers regularly praise its fresh bread, doughnuts, filled rolls and cakes. The bakery successfully balances heritage with modern tastes, making it a popular choice for everything from a quick breakfast to a special weekend treat. It has a rating of 4.8 stars out of 5 on Google based off more than 40 reviews. A staple of March's food scene, Julie's Bakery combines traditional baking with the welcoming atmosphere of a local café. Customers frequently compliment its homemade cakes, pastries and freshly prepared sandwiches, while many review sites highlight the friendly service. Despite its modest size, the bakery has cultivated a fiercely loyal customer base thanks to its commitment to quality and consistency. It's exactly the sort of independent business that thrives on word-of-mouth recommendations. Julie's Bakery boasts a rating of 5 stars out of 5 on Google based off 19 reviews. metadata.title: 5 locations to enjoy autumn walks in Cambridgeshire
metadata.contentSnippet: Whether you're looking for wildlife or a peaceful countryside escape, here are five places to enjoy a picturesque walk in Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 5 locations to enjoy autumn walks in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From misty fenland and colourful woodland to tranquil lakeside trails, Cambridgeshire offers plenty of opportunities to enjoy the best of autumn. Whether you're looking for wildlife or a peaceful countryside escape, here are five places to enjoy a picturesque walk. Autumn is one of the most atmospheric times to visit Wicken Fen National Nature Reserve, one of Britain's oldest nature reserves. Walkers can follow the Four Lodes Trail or Adventurers' Trail through reedbeds, wetlands and open fenland, where grazing Highland cattle and Konik ponies can often be spotted. The Adventurer's Trail is a three-mile circular route, with grazing Highland cattle and Konik ponies among the wildlife visitors may see. As temperatures cool, migratory birds arrive and morning mists frequently hang over the landscape, creating stunning views across the reserve's unique habitat. Few places in Cambridgeshire rival Anglesey Abbey for autumn colour. The National Trust estate is famous for its tree-lined avenues, which transform into spectacular tunnels of gold, orange and red during October and November. Several walking routes wind through the grounds, passing formal gardens, woodland and open parkland. The changing leaves, seasonal flower displays and peaceful atmosphere make it one of the county's most photogenic autumn destinations. Part of Nene Park, Ferry Meadows combines lakes, woodland, riverside paths and open meadows across one of eastern England's largest country parks. Autumn brings vibrant colours to the woodland trails while the park's lakes provide beautiful reflections of the surrounding foliage. With a variety of circular routes available, visitors can enjoy anything from a gentle stroll to a longer waterside walk while taking in the seasonal scenery and wildlife. Located in the Great Ouse Valley, Paxton Pits Nature Reserve offers a mix of lakes, woodland, meadows and riverside footpaths. The reserve is particularly appealing in autumn, when trees around the former gravel pits turn rich shades of amber and bronze. The Heron Trail and Meadow Trail provide excellent opportunities for spotting wildlife, with water birds regularly gathering on the reserve's lakes as the seasons change. Tucked away beside the River Great Ouse in the heart of St Ives, Holt Island Nature Reserve is a hidden gem that feels a world away from the town centre. The reserve's raised boardwalk takes visitors through rare wet woodland, where autumn colours are reflected in the surrounding waterways. Wildlife is abundant throughout the season, and the tranquil setting makes this one of the county's most peaceful walks for anyone looking to escape the bustle of everyday life. metadata.title: 7 hidden beauty spots in Cambridgeshire you may not know exist
metadata.contentSnippet: From tranquil wetlands and historic parkland to famous riverside views and sprawling reservoirs, here are seven beauty spots in Cambridgeshire to visit.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 7 hidden beauty spots in Cambridgeshire you may not know exist
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From tranquil wetlands and historic parkland to famous riverside views and sprawling reservoirs, Cambridgeshire boasts some truly stunning scenery. These seven hidden beauty spots offer the perfect opportunity to experience the county's diverse landscapes. Whether you're seeking a peaceful walk, a family day out or some of the best views East Anglia has to offer, these sites are definitely worth a visit. One of Cambridgeshire's most celebrated natural landscapes, Wicken Fen is the National Trust's oldest nature reserve and one of Europe's most important wetlands. The reserve is home to thousands of species, including rare birds, dragonflies and wild plants. Visitors can explore miles of footpaths, boardwalks and cycling routes through a landscape that has changed little over centuries. Vast skies, peaceful waterways and abundant wildlife make it one of the county's most memorable beauty spots. Covering nearly 1,500 acres, Grafham Water offers some of the most spectacular waterside scenery in Cambridgeshire. The circular trail around the reservoir attracts walkers, runners and cyclists throughout the year. Meanwhile, expansive views across the water create a sense of tranquillity rarely found in the east of England. The site is also popular with birdwatchers, who regularly spot ospreys, grebes and other water birds against the backdrop of one of the county's largest open spaces. Nestled on the banks of the River Great Ouse, Houghton Mill combines beautiful countryside with fascinating history. The 18th-century watermill sits amid riverside meadows, willow-lined paths and charming villages. Visitors can enjoy leisurely walks through Waterclose Meadows, watch boats passing along the river and relax beside one of the most picturesque stretches of water in Cambridgeshire. The idyllic surroundings make it a favourite destination for photographers and walkers alike. Stretching along the River Nene, this vast green space is much more than a city park. Lakes, meadows, woodland and riverside trails combine to create a diverse landscape that attracts visitors throughout the year. At its heart lies Ferry Meadows, where miles of pathways provide opportunities for walking, cycling and wildlife spotting. Arguably the county's most iconic view, The Backs offers stunning vistas of the historic University of Cambridge colleges lining the River Cam. Mature trees, elegant bridges and perfectly maintained lawns combine to create a scene recognised around the world. Whether viewed on foot or from a punt, the area delivers some of the finest scenery in Cambridgeshire and remains a must-visit destination for locals and tourists alike. Famous for its landscaped gardens and extensive grounds, Anglesey Abbey is one of Cambridgeshire's most beautiful historic estates. Visitors can wander through woodland walks, colourful seasonal displays and carefully designed gardens that look spectacular throughout the year. Spring blossom, summer flowers and autumn foliage ensure there is always something worth seeing. As Cambridgeshire's largest country estate, Wimpole Estate offers an impressive combination of grand parkland, lakes, farmland and historic architecture. Visitors can enjoy far-reaching views across rolling countryside, explore woodland trails and discover picturesque corners throughout the estate. Managed by the National Trust, the site provides a striking contrast to the county's landscapes and remains one of the finest places to enjoy the great outdoors. "His gentleness, patience and curiosity help him build strong, positive relationships with students and their families. Plans to build four homes at a former kennels and cattery between Hilton and Fenstanton have been refused after a national planning policy change. The application sought permission to demolish the existing buildings at Fields View, Fenstanton Road, Hilton, and replace them with four detached single-storey homes. The scheme had previously been recommended for approval and was backed by councillors in August, subject to a review against a newly published National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF). Plans to build four homes on the site of a former kennels and cattery between Hilton and Fenstanton have been refused after a change in national planning policy prompted Huntingdonshire District Council officers to reverse their earlier recommendation. (Image: HDC) However, planning officers later concluded that the development should be refused after reassessing it under the updated NPPF 2026. Officers told the council's development management committee that the plans would create "isolated homes" in the countryside outside a settlement boundary. The report stated: "The development would result in the provision of isolated homes outside a settlement and group of dwellings, with no sustainable links to the nearby settlements, resulting in an unsustainable pattern of development." Plans to build four homes on the site of a former kennels and cattery between Hilton and Fenstanton have been refused after a change in national planning policy prompted Huntingdonshire District Council officers to reverse their earlier recommendation. (Image: HDC) Planning officers noted that while the site is previously developed land and Huntingdonshire cannot currently demonstrate a five-year housing land supply, the proposal did not meet the requirements of new NPPF policies relating to development outside settlements. Sylvia Dighton and Dale Robinson applied to redevelop the 0.43-hectare site, which was formerly a boarding kennels and cattery. The business closed during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020 and the site is now vacant. Under the proposal, four four-bedroom bungalows would have been built following demolition of the existing buildings. Plans to build four homes on the site of a former kennels and cattery between Hilton and Fenstanton have been refused after a change in national planning policy prompted Huntingdonshire District Council officers to reverse their earlier recommendation. (Image: HDC) Planning documents stated that the scheme would provide new homes while redeveloping a brownfield site. Highways and environmental health officers, the Environment Agency and the council's emergency planning team raised no objections. However, Hilton Parish Council objected, citing concerns including the site's countryside location, drainage issues and the potential impact on nearby businesses. Three letters of objection were also received from members of the public. Plans to build four homes on the site of a former kennels and cattery between Hilton and Fenstanton have been refused after a change in national planning policy prompted Huntingdonshire District Council officers to reverse their earlier recommendation. (Image: HDC) Officers accepted the scheme would add to the housing supply and support the local economy, but said those benefits did not outweigh its conflict with new national policies. The committee report said the revised NPPF meant the council's Local Plan policy supporting the redevelopment of rural buildings now carried very limited weight where it conflicted with national planning policy. As a result, officers recommended refusal and the application was rejected. Plans to build four homes on the site of a former kennels and cattery between Hilton and Fenstanton have been refused after a change in national planning policy prompted Huntingdonshire District Council officers to reverse their earlier recommendation. (Image: HDC) A previous application for five homes was refused in 2022 because of the site's countryside character and an unsustainable location, before the scheme was reduced to four bungalows.

From the outside, the watering hole looks every bit the picture-postcard English inn. Its historic setting, attractive riverside surroundings and traditional character immediately create a sense of occasion. Step through the door and guests are greeted by a warm and welcoming interior that strikes a careful balance between rustic charm and modern comfort. What really sets The Cock apart, however, is its refined seasonal menus which place emphasis on quality ingredients and modern British cooking. The kitchen delivers dishes that feel more in keeping with an acclaimed restaurant while retaining the relaxed atmosphere people expect from a village pub. The drinks offering is equally impressive. Alongside a well-kept selection of beers and ales, the pub has earned praise for its carefully curated wine list. Whether stopping by for a casual drink in the garden or settling in for a lengthy evening meal, there is a clear focus on quality throughout the experience. One of the pub's biggest strengths is its setting During warmer months, the outdoor space comes into its own, offering a tranquil spot to enjoy food and drink while taking in views of the surrounding countryside and nearby river. It helps create an atmosphere that feels a world away from the bustle of nearby towns and cities. Boasting a Tripadvisor rating of 4.3 out of 5 based off more than 1,250 reviews, the Cock has firmly established itself as one of the county's must-visit pubs. For those seeking superb food, excellent service and an idyllic location, it remains one of the county's finest places to spend an afternoon or evening. One visitor said: "The Cock is one our favourite pubs in a perfect location. An outstanding array of beers, including some local ales, to enjoy in the suntrap of a beer garden.
