metadata.title: UK airline promises to avoid controversial extra charge 'until summer 2028'
metadata.contentSnippet: Jet2 has promised not to introduce fuel surcharges on bookings amid conflict in the Middle East pushing up oil prices

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: UK airline promises to avoid controversial extra charge 'until summer 2028'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Jet2 has pledged not to introduce fuel surcharges on bookings until at least summer 2028. The airline has given customers peace of mind that the price they pay at booking will not change later, even as global oil prices rise due to ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Some airlines have already introduced fuel surcharges to offset these costs. In April, it was reported that Virgin Atlantic added fees, including £50 in economy, £180 in premium economy, and £360 in business class. The surcharges, which can be applied after a booking is confirmed, have drawn criticism from politicians and consumer advocates, who say the charges are unfair and sometimes excessive. Jet2 says it was the first airline to commit to removing the clause in its contract allowing for such a charge, even though it had never applied one. It's claimed its promise will apply to all Jet2 flights and holidays booked through any channel, including online, their mobile app and even independent travel agents. David Hills, chief customer officer at Jet2, said: "Customers work and save hard for their holidays so they deserve certainty from the moment they book. "As they plan their getaways this winter and beyond, we are reaffirming our No Fuel Surcharges guarantee. "We are making it clear that the price customers book with Jet2 is the price they will pay, with no fuel surcharge added later. "That reassurance applies to all customers booking with Jet2, whatever time of year they choose to travel, making now the perfect time to book a well-deserved holiday." Jet2 revealed earlier this year that it will upgrade its passenger experience with new, lightweight seats in 2027. The seats will be installed on its Airbus A321neo aircraft, of which the company has been phasing in more since its arrival a few years ago. Jet2 revealed earlier this year that it will upgrade its passenger experience with new, lightweight seats in 2027. (Image: PA) The aircraft has two engines and one aisle, with rows of seats on either side. It can carry up to 244 people, depending on its layout. New engines and curved wingtips, known as “sharklets”, help reduce fuel use and carbon dioxide emissions compared with older aircraft. The Airbus A321neo is also recognised as the most fuel-efficient aircraft in its class. It reduces fuel consumption and CO2 emissions per seat by over 20% and provides a 50% lower noise footprint compared to the current fleet average. The airline reached 30 operational A321neo aircraft by mid-2026, while documents show 124 more are scheduled for delivery by 2035. Plans to turn offices in St Ives into 16 flats have been given the go-ahead by Huntingdonshire District Council. The council has granted prior approval for the conversion of Units 5 and 6 at Meadow Park, Meadow Lane, from offices into residential accommodation. The application was submitted by Allgood Services Ltd. The scheme will create 12 one-bedroom flats and four two-bedroom flats across the ground, first and second floors. The flats will have a combined internal floor area of about 852 square metres. In its decision, Huntingdonshire District Council confirmed that prior approval was "required and approved", subject to a series of conditions. The development must be completed within three years of the approval date. Huntingdonshire District Council has granted prior approval for the conversion of Units 5 and 6 at Meadow Park, Meadow Lane, from offices into residential accommodation. (Image: HDC) Planning officers said the scheme met the rules for converting commercial buildings into homes under permitted development rights. The proposals include 32 car parking spaces, effectively two for each flat, as well as covered storage for 20 bicycles. The existing vehicle access from Meadow Lane will remain. Cambridgeshire County Council’s highways team raised no objection, saying the existing access could handle traffic from the new homes. The site was also considered to be in a sustainable location, with pedestrian links towards St Ives town centre. Huntingdonshire District Council has granted prior approval for the conversion of Units 5 and 6 at Meadow Park, Meadow Lane, from offices into residential accommodation. (Image: HDC) The council’s environmental health team raised no objections over contamination or noise. Officers said the site is in Flood Zone 1, although part of the parking area faces a surface-water flood risk. The building itself is outside the risk area. Every habitable room would have a window for natural light, and officers said the flats meet national space standards. No public representations had been received when the application was determined. Cadent also raised no objection, while the Environment Agency said it had no comments to make. The approval follows other conversions from offices to homes within Meadow Park. Planning documents say 18 flats had already been approved through conversions elsewhere on the estate, including at 3 and 4 Meadow Park. Separate permission was granted on September 17, 2026, for external works to Units 5 and 6, including four dormers and changes to windows and cladding. The latest prior approval does not itself authorise external alterations to the building.

metadata.title: State pension age could be cut to 65 to help free up jobs for young
metadata.contentSnippet: A petition calling for the UK state pension age to be cut to 65 for everyone has passed 100,000 signatures

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: State pension age could be cut to 65 to help free up jobs for young
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A petition calling for the state pension age to be reduced to 65 for everyone has passed 100,000 signatures, triggering consideration for a debate in Parliament. The campaign argues that lowering the state pension age could allow older people to retire with dignity, avoid financial hardship and free up jobs for younger workers entering the labour market. The petition, created by Michelle Gill, has attracted 100,769 signatures and remains open until March 16, 2027. It calls for the current state pension age to be reduced to 65, arguing that people aged 65 to 67 can face poor health, caring responsibilities and limited employment opportunities while waiting to qualify for their state pension. The campaign argues that forcing people to work longer can be unfair for those who are struggling with their health or unable to find suitable employment. It also suggests that allowing older workers to retire earlier could create more opportunities for younger people trying to get into work. The petition passed the 100,000-signature threshold, meaning the Petitions Committee will consider it for debate in Parliament. An update published on October 24, 2026, confirmed the milestone. However, reaching the threshold does not guarantee that a debate will take place, nor does it mean the Government has agreed to change the state pension age. In fact, earlier this month they made a statement, saying: "The Government has no plans to lower the State Pension age." They added: "State Pension age is now gradually rising from 66 to 67. "This increase began in April 2026 and will complete in March 2028. "Increases to State Pension age have been in legislation since the Pensions Act 1995. "As longevity has increased and our society aged, State Pension age rises have maintained fairness between generations and protected the public finances." The petition remains open for people to sign until March 16, 2027. Do you think the state pension age should be reduced to 65 for everyone? Tell us in the comments below...

Quality Bites, established in May 2013, was a halal frozen food brand that offered a range of ethnic frozen foods including samosas, kebabs, and crispy chicken. The company described itself as "one of the leading manufacturers of ethnic foods in the UK". Quality Bites worked with retailers, wholesalers, and distributors nationwide, supplying products to more than 1,000 independent supermarkets and grocery stores. After 13 years in business, Quality Bites has now entered liquidation and closed. The company was voluntarily wound up on October 7, according to The Gazette. Deviesh Raikundalia of Hall Chadwick (UK) Limited has been appointed as liquidator. It has been a tough year for the UK high street, with several retailers entering administration or liquidation and others announcing widespread store closures. Major high street brands Claire's and Quiz have been forced to close all their remaining stores after falling into administration. UK fashion retailer Leading Labels is also set to close its remaining 15 stores after falling into liquidation in May. Whitbread closed all its standalone branded restaurants across the UK last month, affecting five brands: However, Queensway Inns and Common Table Group have now taken over 110 of these former Whitbread sites, saving them from closure. TG Jones and the British Heart Foundation will also be closing around 150 stores each across the UK. Wynsors World of Shoes is shutting 17 stores across the UK, with closing down sales already underway at several affected branches. UK entertainment retailer Zavvi has ceased trading after nearly 20 years, having collapsed into administration for a second time. Australian stationery retailer Typo is also set to pull out of the UK in 2027, closing all its stores and ending online trading. Other retailers have been forced to close stores this year, including: Several UK travel companies have ceased trading or entered administration in 2026, including: Wayfairer Travel Limited has also suspended all services "until further notice" as it looks to appoint an administrator. Meanwhile, four UK airlines have fallen into administration or liquidation: Meanwhile, UK delivery company Yodel was phased out completely in July after being acquired by InPost. Iconic fashion brand Nasty Gal has also shut down its website after being sold by Debenhams in a deal worth around £12 million (US$16 million). It hasn't all been bad news for the UK high street, with several major brands announcing new store openings for 2026, including Joules, B&M, Aldi, M&S, and Superdrug. Saturday night's (October 24) main show saw Tabby Stoecker and Mark Karmalita top the leaderboard with a score of 37. Meanwhile, Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis Warr were left at the bottom on 17 points. The leaderboard each week is decided by the judges' scores, which are weighted equally with votes from the public, meaning in theory anyone could end up in the dreaded dance-off. Wright-Phillips and Warr were one of the pairs who ended up in the dance-off, along with Jaime Winstone and Carlos Gu, who came third from bottom on the night with a score of 24. Winstone and Gu repeated their foxtrot to Man I Need by Olivia Dean, while Wright-Phillips and Warr reprised their jive to Faith by Stevie Wonder featuring Ariana Grande. Judges Craig Revel Horwood and Motsi Mabuse voted to save Winstone and Gu, but head judge Shirley Ballas voted for Wright-Phillips and Warr. This left it up to Anton Du Beke, who had this week's casting vote. Shaun Wright-Phillips and Alexis Warr ended up being eliminated in Week 5 (Image: Guy Levy/BBC) In the end, he decided to save Winstone and Gu, meaning that Wright-Phillips and Warr went home. Sunday night's results also came with the announcement that there would be a triple dance-off for next week's Halloween episode. The three couples with the lowest combined judges’ scores and public votes will dance again next week, before the judges eliminate one pair. Strictly will then return to a two-couple dance-off for the rest of the series. Shaun Wright-Phillips is a former footballer who played for the likes of Chelsea, Manchester City and Queens Park Rangers during his career. Since retiring, he has worked as a football commentator for BBC Sport, ITV Sport, Talksport and Sky Sports. His father is the former footballer and pundit Ian Wright, who adopted him when he was three, after beginning a relationship with his mother, Sharon Phillips. metadata.title: Millions of TV users urged to make 1 change this week or lose films and shows
metadata.contentSnippet: Millions of TV users could lose any purchased films or TV box sets this week if they don't make one change before November 1.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Millions of TV users urged to make 1 change this week or lose films and shows
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of TV users could lose their purchased films or box sets if they don’t complete one simple task this week. Virgin Media TV customers who use the Virgin Media Store to buy films and TV shows must act now if they want to keep their purchased content. Anyone who has used the store to buy content will no longer be able to do so from Sunday, November 1, as it is set to close. Virgin Media TV has warned its customers to move their purchased content over to a Rakuten TV account to keep it. If you don’t make the switch, you can expect to lose access to your purchases since the Virgin Media Store will be closed and will no longer work for customers after the cut-off date. Virgin Media said: “Virgin Media Store is closing. “Rakuten TV is the new home for the movies and TV box sets you’ve bought from us.” If you make the switch to a Rakuten TV account, you can buy your films and TV box sets via the app, which can be accessed on your Virgin TV box. You can set up an account and transfer content now, and Virgin Media TV urges you to do this “as soon as you can”. However, customers can still use the Virgin Media Store to buy films and box sets until November 1. If you want to rent content from the Virgin Media Store, you still can, as rentals will not change, Virgin Media has reassured customers. To transfer your content to Rakuten TV, you’ll need to sign in to the Virgin Media Store and choose the 'transfer to Rakuten TV' option. Follow the instructions given on screen to transfer the content, and then a Rakuten TV account will be created for you if you haven’t already got one. If you do have an account, you’ll be able to log in to access the transferred films and box sets. Once you’ve followed the above steps, you’ll be able to watch the transferred content via the Rakuten TV app on your Virgin TV. Recommended reading: If you have never bought any films or TV box sets from the Virgin Media Store, you won’t need to do anything. The changeover only concerns customers who have bought content from the store. What's your favourite film? Tell us in the comments below.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 5 cinemas in Cambridgeshire we have loved and lost
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From grand art deco picture houses to busy town-centre screens, cinemas were once at the heart of communities across Cambridgeshire. While modern multiplexes have taken their place, many former venues are still remembered by residents who spent countless evenings watching films there. Here's five cinemas we have loved and lost. The Grand Cinema began life in Huntingdon's former Corn Exchange and officially opened as a cinema on 1 January 1913. It survived a devastating fire in 1954 and reopened later that same year with modern facilities and a new screen. For decades it served as a popular entertainment venue in the town. The cinema eventually closed in August 1964, after which the building was used for bingo before redevelopment. The Princess Cinema was another venue that once played a prominent role in Peterborough's recreation and leisure scene. The single floor cinema opened in 1929 and welcomed countless visitors during a time when a night at the cinema was among the most popular forms of entertainment. Odeon Theatres Ltd eventually bought the Princess Cinema in 1936 before it was leased to J.F. Emery Circuit of Manchester in 1937. It closed in March 1958 with “Son of the Hunchback” and Charlie Chaplin in “The Kid”. The Playhouse Cinema served Cambridge residents during the heyday of traditional picture houses. It became the second cinema on Mill Road in 1913 when a brand new building was created. Like many cinemas of its era, it provided affordable entertainment and a shared community experience before television became widespread. Although little remains of the building today, the Playhouse occupies a notable place in Cambridge's cultural and entertainment heritage. The Hippodrome Cinema was arguably Huntingdon's most fondly remembered picture house. Opening in 1933 with more than 800 seats and a then state-of-the-art Western Electric sound system, it became a popular destination for generations of local cinemagoers. Located close to the town centre, it remained a prominent entertainment venue for decades. Films were dropped in favour of bingo in 1971 before briefly returning, but the cinema ultimately closed and was demolished around 1977 to make way for retail development. The Exchange Cinema was once among several cinemas serving Ely residents during the peak years of cinema-going. Situated in the cathedral city, it provided local audiences with access to the latest film releases at a time when trips to the pictures were a major social event. It closed in 1963 before being demolished in 1964 and remains part of Ely's rich cultural and entertainment heritage. Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: 7 beloved shops that have disappeared from Cambridgeshire's high streets
metadata.contentSnippet: From iconic department stores to beloved chains, here are seven shops that have disappeared from Cambridgeshire's high streets.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 7 beloved shops that have disappeared from Cambridgeshire's high streets
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From iconic department stores to beloved high street chains, many familiar shops have disappeared from Cambridgeshire in recent years. So, here are seven popular stores across the county that we have loved and lost. The Peterborough branch of Beales occupied the prominent Westgate department store building and became a major city-centre retailer. The original Beales store traded there for around nine years before the chain entered administration in 2020. A revived Beales reopened in the building in May 2021, employing around 30 staff, but the store announced its closure in October 2022 and finally shut in January 2023. The building has since been earmarked for redevelopment. For years, BHS was one of Peterborough's best-known department stores, selling clothing, homeware and electrical goods. The retailer itself was founded in 1928 and became a staple of high streets nationwide. The Peterborough branch was among hundreds affected when the company collapsed into administration in 2016. The store closed during the national shutdown of the chain, bringing an end to a familiar shopping destination for local residents. The Huntingdon branch of Woolworths was a favourite for everything from toys and music to stationery and the famous pick-and-mix sweets. Founded nationally in 1909, Woolworths became one of Britain's most recognisable high-street chains. Like all UK branches, the Huntingdon store closed during the company's collapse in late 2008 and early 2009. For many residents, its closure marked the end of an era on the town's high street. Founded in 1904 by Frank Brittain, Brittains Furnishers was one of St Neots' oldest surviving independent retailers. Originally based in Eaton Ford, the business later moved to the High Street in 1924 and became a trusted destination for furniture and home furnishings. After 120 years of trading, the family-run company announced its closure in 2023, citing online competition, rising costs and changing consumer habits. Ely's Woolworths traced its roots back to a purpose-built store opened in 1935 on Fore Street before relocating to Market Place in the early 2000s. The branch became a popular feature of city-centre shopping before closing in December 2008 as part of the chain's nationwide collapse. The prominent Market Place store has since housed other retailers, but many residents still remember it as Woolworths. The Wisbech branch of Bonmarché, located at 9-10 High Street, served shoppers for many years before closing around 2019. The premises subsequently remained vacant for several years before redevelopment plans emerged. The building itself has a long retail history dating back more than a century, having previously housed drapers and the former Bainbridges Department Store. The Peterborough branch of Debenhams was a cornerstone of the city centre for decades, attracting shoppers looking for fashion, beauty products and homewares. The retailer itself was founded in 1778, and the Peterborough store became one of the city's best-known department stores. Following the chain's collapse, Debenhams began winding down its UK operations in 2021, with stores closing nationwide as the business left the high street for good. metadata.title: 9 hidden gems in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire is packed with hidden gems that rarely make the county's tourism brochures.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 9 hidden gems in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire is packed with hidden gems that rarely make the county's tourism brochures. From ancient wetlands and secret nature reserves to forgotten archaeological sites and historic country estates, here are nine lesser-known attractions to visit. Often described as a hidden gem, Wicken Fen is the National Trust's oldest nature reserve and one of Europe's most important wetlands. Visitors can explore boardwalks winding through reedbeds, marshes and wildflower meadows while spotting dragonflies, rare birds and grazing Highland cattle. The reserve offers a glimpse into the ancient Fenland landscape that once dominated the region, making it an excellent destination for walkers, families and wildlife enthusiasts. Hidden away between Peterborough and Huntingdon, Holme Fen feels remarkably wild and remote. The reserve is home to the famous Holme Post, marking Britain's lowest land point at around 2.75 metres below sea level. Visitors can explore peaceful woodland trails, wetlands and bird hides while discovering a fascinating story of how drainage transformed the Fens. One of Britain's last remaining washlands, Nene Washes offers spectacular wildlife viewing throughout the year. Winter floods attract thousands of migratory birds, while spring and summer bring breeding cranes, godwits and marsh harriers. Birdwatchers rate it among the county's finest locations, yet it remains surprisingly under the radar with many local visitors. Covering hundreds of acres beside the River Nene, the park combines lakes, woodland, meadows and cycle routes. Families can enjoy water sports, miniature railways, walking trails and abundant wildlife. Created from former gravel workings, Paxton Pits has become one of Cambridgeshire's most important wildlife sites. Its lakes, reedbeds and woodland attract kingfishers, otters and hundreds of bird species throughout the year. Well-maintained trails and viewing hides make it accessible for families, photographers and nature lovers alike. Many visitors compare the reserve favourably with much larger national wildlife attractions while enjoying a quieter atmosphere. One of the most significant Bronze Age archaeological sites in Britain, Flag Fen remains surprisingly little known outside the region. The attraction centres on a 3,500-year-old causeway preserved beneath the peat and waterlogged soils of the Fens. Interactive exhibits, reconstructed roundhouses and fascinating artefacts help bring prehistoric Cambridgeshire to life. One of the largest habitat restoration projects in the country, Ouse Fen offers expansive wetland scenery and exceptional birdwatching opportunities. Visitors can enjoy peaceful walking trails through reedbeds and lakes while looking out for cranes, bitterns and marsh harriers. The sheer scale of the reserve creates an extraordinary sense of isolation, despite being only a short distance from Ely and nearby villages. Tucked inside Huntingdon's former grammar school, the Cromwell Museum tells the story of Oliver Cromwell and the English Civil War through a collection of nationally important artefacts. Despite its historical significance, it remains relatively overlooked compared with larger museums in Cambridge. Visitors can examine weapons, portraits and personal items linked to one of Britain's most influential and controversial historical figures. Located just outside Peterborough, Sacrewell blends history, countryside and family-friendly attractions. Highlights include a restored 19th-century watermill, rare farm animals, woodland walks and seasonal events. The setting offers a gentler and quieter alternative to larger commercial attractions while still providing plenty to keep children entertained. Its combination of heritage and outdoor space makes it particularly appealing for multi-generational visits. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Hardest primary schools to get your child a place in
metadata.contentSnippet: The hardest primary schools in Cambridgeshire to get your child a place in have been revealed in new data. Most schools are able to offer a place to every student who picked them as their top preference, but some don’t have enough for everyone.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hardest primary schools to get your child a place in
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The hardest primary schools in Cambridgeshire to get your child a place in have been revealed in new data. Most schools are able to offer a place to every student who picked them as their top preference, but some don’t have enough for everyone. In 2026, the most oversubscribed primary school was Milton Road Primary School in Cambridge with 62.5 per cent of students who picked it as their first choice given a place. This was followed by Ridgefield Primary School in Cambridge which had enough places for 69.8 per cent of first preferences and Abbots Ripton Primary School near Huntingdon which had 70.8 per cent. Ridgefield had 43 first preferences for 30 places and Abbots Ripton had 24 students put it as their first preference – but only 17 places on offer. The school with the most first preferences was Milton Road Primary School, which had 60 places but 96 students picking it as their top choice. Milton Road was also the most oversubscribed school in 2025, when 113 students chose it as their first choice and only 53 per cent were successful. It was followed by Newnham Croft Primary School in Cambridge, with 56.6 per cent of students successful, and St Alban’s Catholic Primary School in Cambridge at 60 per cent. Meldreth Primary School was the most oversubscribed in 2024, when 65 per cent of 46 first preferences were offered one of the school’s 30 places. It was followed by Holywell Primary School in Needingworth, near St Ives, at 69.8 per cent and Houghton Primary School in Wyton, near Huntingdon, at 71.4 per cent. This year, 94.7 per cent of Cambridgeshire children were given a place at their first preference school – and 98.9 per cent at one of their top three preferred schools. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said that, with just over one per cent allocated a place outside their preferences, it was the “second lowest proportion recorded in the last five years”. They said: “We’re committed to providing the best possible start in life for young people in our county and access to high quality education close to home is key. “With population centres changing over time around our growing county, the council’s Education team work hard, in partnership with schools and with careful reference to pupil forecasting figures, to try and ensure we can offer the right numbers of school places, in the right areas, when they are needed.” If your child was born between September 1, 2022, and August 31, 2023, and you live in Cambridgeshire, you will need to apply for a place in Reception for September 2027. This can be done on the county council’s website here, and the deadline for applications is January 15, 2027.

metadata.title: Tributes pour in to 'kind young man' who died in lorry crash
metadata.contentSnippet: Tributes have poured in to a young motorcyclist, described as a "kind young man", who tragically died in a Sawtry crash involving a lorry.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Tributes pour in to 'kind young man' who died in lorry crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Tributes have poured in to a young motorcyclist, described as a "kind young man", who tragically died in a crash involving a lorry. Friends and neighbours have shared memories of 23-year-old Tyler Ellis from Yaxley after The Hunts Post opened a book of condolence. Mr Ellis was riding a black Kawasaki motorbike when it collided with a red Volvo HGV. The crash happened on the B1043 Old North Road in Sawtry at about 12.50pm on October 5. Mr Ellis died at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge the following day. He was described by those who knew him as kind, fun, and deeply missed. Melanie Bradley said: "We have such wonderful memories of Tyler growing up in Yaxley. "He really was such a handsome and kind young man, my thoughts are with all his family and friends. "Words don't sound enough to bring comfort to you all. "So so sorry you had to lose Tyler." Others spoke of his humour and the lasting impression he left on those around him. Harvey Cousins said: "Goodbye my dear friend, I love you bro. "Thank you for all the funny memories, you will never be forgotten." James Weech said: "Rest in peace my friend. "We all miss you terribly mate and will hold onto the memories for the rest of our lives." People who had known Tyler since childhood also paid tribute. Nicola Hendrick said: "R.I.P. Tyler. I have fond memories of you whilst I worked at Stretton pre school where you attended. "Thinking of all the family at this very sad time." Domenica Ciniero said: "Tyler, I will miss our cinema dates and pub nights. "You were always such a sweet and fun presence to have around. "I will miss playing games with you and you winning every single time. "Life will always feel different and you will always be missed. "Rest in peace and my sincerest condolences to your amazing family, friends and colleagues." Tyler's family described him as a "beautiful, loving son" with an infectious laugh and a smile that could light up any room.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two community radio stations have begun broadcasting on DAB digital radio across St Neots and Huntingdon. Ouse Valley Radio and Black Cat Radio, both well-established stations in the region, teamed up for a successful joint bid to secure the small-scale DAB licence. The stations worked closely with Cambridge Digital Radio Ltd to launch their digital broadcasts. Tony Obee, CEO of Ouse Valley Radio, said: "Ouse Valley Radio's history goes back to 2011, and over the years we have developed a distinctive mix of community and specialist broadcasting. Black Cat Radio (Image: Ouse Valley Radio) "Our Over to You community access programme has championed the work of hundreds of local charities and community groups, while programmes such as our award-winning radio soap Huntsford, Ouse Valley Today local current affairs show and the acclaimed astronomy programme The Sky Tonight reflect our commitment to informing, entertaining and inspiring listeners. "We are also proud to broadcast specialist music programmes covering various genres including Classical Music, Jazz, and Country. "We are delighted to have worked alongside Black Cat Radio on this joint enterprise, bringing greater listener choice across the region through DAB." The Ouse Valley Radio DAB aerial array at Godmanchester (Image: Ouse Valley Radio) The stations have installed new equipment at broadcast sites in Godmanchester and on Paxton Hill overlooking St Neots. Ste Greenall of Black Cat Radio said: "As community stations, manned by volunteers, we strive to bring a professsional sound to our programming. "Ultimately, the success of any radio station is down to its listeners. "Whilst we are competing with each other and indeed with the BBC and independent sector, our strengths lie in engaging with our audiences. "We have received further nominations in the Community Radio Awards this year, including the subject of prostate cancer awareness." Ouse Valley Radio (Image: Ouse Valley Radio) He said: "We were delighted to work alongside Black Cat and Ouse Valley Radio throughout the entire project lifecycle, from the initial application through to planning, construction, and installation. "It's exciting to see the multiplex launch, and we look forward to continuing to provide the technical services and support needed to ensure its successful ongoing operation." Both stations remain available on FM, online, through smart speakers, and via their mobile apps.

metadata.title: Chest infection or cold? Boots pharmacist shares key signs and when to see a GP
metadata.contentSnippet: Boots pharmacist shares chest infection symptoms, recovery advice and warning signs.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Chest infection or cold? Boots pharmacist shares key signs and when to see a GP
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: As coughs, colds and flu become more common during the colder months, it can sometimes be difficult to know whether you're dealing with a common seasonal illness or a chest infection. Chest infections can develop after a cold or flu and share some of the same symptoms. However, there are certain signs people can look out for, according to a pharmacist. Boots has shared advice on spotting a possible chest infection as the retailer launches a private Chest Infection Service in more than 90 stores across the UK. Claire Nevinson, Superintendent Pharmacist at Boots, said symptoms of a chest infection can include a chesty cough producing coloured mucus, wheezing, shortness of breath and chest discomfort. Other possible symptoms include a high temperature, headaches, aching muscles and tiredness. She explained: "A chest infection is an infection of the lungs or large airways and they often follow a cold or flu, therefore symptoms can be similar. "Symptoms of a chest infection may include a chesty cough with coloured mucus, wheezing and shortness of breath, chest discomfort, a high temperature, headaches, aching muscles and tiredness." According to the Boots pharmacist, symptoms will often get better without treatment within seven to 10 days, although a cough can remain for as long as three weeks. People should seek medical advice from a GP if a cough lasts for longer than three weeks or they are coughing up blood. There are several things people can do at home to help ease symptoms. Nevinson recommends getting plenty of rest, drinking enough fluids and eating a healthy, balanced diet. Sleeping with your head raised or using extra pillows may also make breathing easier. Anyone whose symptoms persist, has had a cough for more than three weeks or is coughing up blood should seek medical attention from a GP, according to the pharmacist's advice. Some people are at greater risk of developing a serious chest infection. Nevinson said this includes babies and young children, older people, pregnant women, people who smoke, those with long-term respiratory conditions such as asthma and people with weakened immune systems. The advice comes as Boots launches a private Chest Infection Service for people aged 16 and over at more than 90 stores. Appointments last 20 minutes and involve an assessment by an independent prescribing pharmacist, who can offer advice and discuss treatment options. These could include over-the-counter medicines or, where considered appropriate, a course of antibiotics. Recommended Reading Nevinson said: "Chest infections are particularly common during the colder months and can leave people feeling unwell and unsure about the best course of action. "Our new Chest Infection Service provides customers with convenient access to advice, support and treatment right on the high street." The consultation costs £25, with prescribed medicines or over-the-counter treatments charged separately. Customers can book online through Boots and pay in store.

metadata.title: Aerial photos show proposed site of discount retailer's first Hunts store
metadata.contentSnippet: Aerial photos have captured the proposed site of a Home Bargain's first store in Huntingdonshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Aerial photos show proposed site of discount retailer's first Hunts store
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Aerial photos have captured the site where a popular discount retailer hopes to build its first store in Huntingdonshire. Applicant TJ Morris Limited, which trades as Home Bargains, has lodged plans for a new retail unit on St Peters Road. If approved, the "comprehensive development" would also provide customer and service access, car parking and landscaping. The site is surrounded by retail and commercial buildings, including Bensons for Beds and Wickes retail stores to the north. It is currently an "undeveloped plot" presenting an "opportunity to deliver a planned commercial scheme," a design and access statement said. The site would comprise more than 24,500 square feet, excluding an external garden centre According to the plans, the "high-quality" development would re-purpose the site, providing local people "with choice and quality of provision". The proposed development would also create new full and part-time jobs while creating an "attractive and welcoming environment". Comprising more 24,500 square feet, the store would feature an additional 7,500 square-foot garden centre. It would feature composite cladding at the upper level with brick work below and glazed shopfronts in keeping with the retailer's branding. Spread across one storey, the store would "reutilise and modify an existing access point from St Peters Road.” A planning and retail statement submitted as part of the application highlighted Home Bargains' "aggressive expansion strategy". Documents outlining the chain's retail requirements for 2024-25 said its ongoing success was "built on the offer of top brands at bottom prices". The proposed development would "deliver a number of significant benefits to the local economy", the plans added. This includes "supporting the vitality and viability of the local retail offer" and "enhancement of retail choice and qualitative retail offer". "The development represents a substantial investment in Huntingdon that will ensure the delivery of a high-quality and modern retail building and wider site improvements. "The proposals will also secure the long-term occupation of the site, create new jobs and will result in significant investment both directly and indirectly in the local economy." metadata.title: 10 Cambridgeshire fireworks displays to visit this Bonfire Night
metadata.contentSnippet: Find 10 of the best Bonfire Night fireworks displays in Cambridgeshire, including Cambridge, Ely, Huntingdon, Duxford and Peterborough.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 Cambridgeshire fireworks displays to visit this Bonfire Night
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: It's almost that time of year again when Cambridgeshire night skies light up in bright colours to mark Bonfire Night. More than 400 years ago, Guy Fawkes was caught attempting to blow up the Houses of Parliament in the now notorious Gunpowder Plot. Here are 10 of the best Cambridgeshire fireworks displays to visit this year to mark the occasion. Cambridge City Council’s annual fireworks event takes place at Midsummer Common, one of the county’s largest free displays. The event starts at 6pm on November 5, with fireworks at 7pm. Fairytale Fireworks at Huntingdon Racecourse features fireworks, rides and food stalls. The event takes place on Saturday, October 24, and bookings are open now. Kimbolton Castle provides the historic backdrop for a fireworks show and entertainment village. This year’s display starts at 5.45pm on Friday, November 6. Adult tickets cost £15.95, while children under five go free. Cherry Hill Park hosts Ely’s annual fireworks display, with family entertainment and refreshments. Gates open at 5pm on Saturday, November 7, and the fireworks start at 7pm. Cambourne Fireworks at Great Cambourne Cricket Pitches features funfair rides and food stalls. The event starts at 6.30pm on Friday, November 6. Soham Town Rangers Football & Social Club hosts a community fireworks display with fairground rides and refreshments. Doors open at 5pm on Friday, November 6, and tickets cost from £6. The Big Field hosts Hemingford Fireworks, a community bonfire and fireworks event with entertainment and street food. Gates open at 4.30pm on Saturday, November 7, followed by a bonfire at 5.30pm and fireworks at 7pm. Grafham Village Hall hosts a village fireworks celebration, with food and drink available on site. Tickets are almost sold out for this year’s display on Saturday, November 7. Imperial War Museum Duxford hosts a family-friendly fireworks night on its historic airfield. Adult tickets cost from £15, and doors open at 4.30pm on Thursday, November 5. The Embankment hosts a major fireworks event with professional displays and entertainment. Gates open at 5pm on Saturday, November 7, and the event ends at 10pm.

metadata.title: Police issue fresh update on pair arrested after death of three-month old baby
metadata.contentSnippet: Police have issued a fresh update on a man and woman arrested after the death of a three-month-old baby March, Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Police issue fresh update on pair arrested after death of three-month old baby
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have issued a fresh update on a man and woman arrested after the death of a three-month-old baby in Cambridgeshire. Atijus Elertaite was rushed to hospital in a life-threatening condition after officers were called to St John's Chase, March, at just after 11am on January 3. Prior to his death, a 25-year-old woman and 22-year-old man, both from March, were arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm. They were also arrested on suspicion of possessing class B and class C drugs and were released on bail. Atijus tragically died in hospital on January 8 and a post-mortem examination gave a preliminary cause of death as a head injury. The pair were re-arrested on suspicion of murder on January 22 and were released on bail until April 2. They were then re-bailed until April 22 before this was extended to July 22 and then until October 22. In July, Cambridgeshire Constabulary revealed it had taken no further action against against the pair for the grievous bodily harm offence. In an update on Thursday, the force confirmed the man and woman have had their bail extended for a fourth time until March 22, 2027. An inquest on March 12 at Vantage House, in Huntingdon, revealed the circumstances surrounding the baby's death. Area coroner for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Elizabeth Gray revealed Atijus had been found not breathing by his parents. Paramedics attended an address on St John's Chase and managed to revive the toddler after 90 minutes of resuscitation, the court heard. Atijus was transferred to Addenbrooke's Hospital, in Cambridge, where tests revealed he had a "bleed on the brain." Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: 9 of the best Sunday lunch spots worth travelling across Cambridgeshire for
metadata.contentSnippet: Nothing rounds off the weekend quite like a traditional Sunday lunch and Cambridgeshire has plenty of standout options.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 9 of the best Sunday lunch spots worth travelling across Cambridgeshire for
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nothing rounds off the weekend quite like a traditional Sunday lunch. Whether you fancy perfectly cooked beef, towering Yorkshire puddings or a classic carvery piled high with vegetables, Cambridgeshire has plenty of standout options. Here are nine of the best spots across the county to enjoy a Sunday roast. Widely regarded as one of the finest pub restaurants in the Peterborough area, The Black Horse combines a picturesque village setting with generous Sunday roasts and attentive service. Diners regularly praise the quality of the beef and lamb, while roast potatoes, Yorkshire puddings and seasonal vegetables help complete the traditional experience. The cosy interior and garden seating make it particularly popular for family get-togethers on a Sunday. It boasts a score of 4.5 stars out of 5 on Google based off more than 860 reviews. Best known for its farm shop, butchery and family attraction, Johnsons of Old Hurst is also home to a highly regarded Sunday carvery. Much of the meat comes directly from the business's own butchery, giving diners excellent quality and provenance. Expect generous portions, plenty of vegetables and traditional trimmings. Its family-friendly setting makes it a favourite destination for a leisurely Sunday afternoon. The Steakhouse boasts a rating of 4.6 out of 5 stars on Google based off more than 260 reviews. Set inside a 17th-century coaching inn, The Three Kings has built a strong reputation for its Great British Sunday Roast. Visitors regularly praise the generous portions, homemade roast potatoes and welcoming atmosphere. Exposed beams, open fireplaces and a traditional pub feel add to the charm, making it a popular choice for diners travelling from Ely and surrounding villages. It boasts a rating of 4.3 stars out of 5 on Google based off mor than 480 reviews. This award-winning country inn near Cambridge serves one of the county's most highly regarded Sunday lunches. Diners can enjoy quality roast meats, seasonal vegetables and carefully sourced local ingredients in a Grade II-listed setting full of character. Original timber beams, open fireplaces and attentive service make it an ideal destination for those seeking a more upmarket Sunday dining experience. The Crown & Punchbowl boasts a rating of 4.6 stars out of 5 on Google based off more than 1,000 reviews. Dating back to the 15th century, The Hole in the Wall is renowned for its traditional Sunday roasts served in a charming rural setting. Guests can choose from several roast meat options alongside homemade Yorkshire puddings and classic accompaniments. The historic surroundings and strong reputation for high-quality food make it a favourite among Cambridge-area food lovers. It boasts a rating of 4.6 stars out of 5 on Google based off more than 500 reviews. For those who love a classic carvery, Hartford Mill remains one of the county's most reliable choices. Diners can select from a range of meats including beef, turkey and gammon, accompanied by all the traditional trimmings. Known for its excellent value and substantial portions, it consistently attracts locals looking for a hearty Sunday lunch without breaking the bank. It has a rating of 4.3 stars out 5 on Google based off more than 4,300 reviews. The Clarendon Arms has developed a loyal following thanks to its carefully prepared Sunday roasts and traditional pub atmosphere. Slow-roast pork, quality beef and lamb feature regularly, while booking ahead is strongly advised due to its popularity. The pub's reputation for quality ingredients and well-executed comfort food has made it one of Cambridge's standout Sunday lunch venues. metadata.contentSnippet: As Halloween approaches, Cambridgeshire's history has spawned countless ghost stories and reports of paranormal encounters in pubs across the county.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 Cambridgeshire pubs where the spirits might not all be behind the bar
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: As Halloween approaches, Cambridgeshire's history has spawned countless ghost stories and reports of paranormal encounters in pubs across the county. From ghostly monks and phantom sailors to heartbroken lovers and mysterious ladies in white, some pubs are serving up more than just pints and pub grub. The county is packed with historic inns whose centuries-old walls have become the setting for enduring tales of paranormal activity, making them popular stops for both ghost hunters and curious drinkers alike. Here are some of Cambridgeshire's most haunted pubs, whether you believe the stories or not. Arguably Cambridgeshire's most famous haunted pub, The Old Ferry Boat Inn is linked to the ghost of Juliet Tewsley, a young woman said to have died after a tragic love affair in 1050. Legend claims her grave lies beneath the pub and that her spirit returns each year on the anniversary of her death. Staff and customers have reported lights refusing to switch off, cold spots and unexplained noises. The Golden Lion in St Ives has accumulated several ghost stories over the years. Reports include the mysterious Green Lady. (Image: Google Maps/Street View) The historic coaching inn in St Ives has accumulated several ghost stories over the years. Reports include the mysterious Green Lady, said to haunt rooms 12 and 13, while some guests have claimed to encounter the ghost of Oliver Cromwell, who is said to appear on the 13th of every month. This centuries-old hotel and pub near Ely Cathedral has a reputation for spectral visitors. Stories describe sightings of a young girl, a maid and a former landlord, along with reports of footsteps and icy cold areas within the building. Situated beside the River Great Ouse, The Cutter Inn has been linked to stories of a former landlady whose apparition has allegedly been seen by staff and visitors. People have also reported catching the scent of perfume with no obvious source. Peterborough's famous coaching inn is said to be haunted by several spirits. Guests and staff have reported hearing footsteps and jangling keys, while stories also tell of a ghostly dog connected to a long-forgotten accident. Infamous highwayman Dick Turpin is said to be among the spirits who haunt The Bell Inn at Stilton near Peterborough. (Image: Google Maps/Street View) According to local paranormal folklore, the ghost of infamous highwayman Dick Turpin is said to haunt this historic coaching inn. A mysterious Lady in Grey and the ghost of writer Daniel Defoe are all said to haunt The Bell Inn, with lots of poltergeist activity throughout the hostelry. The apparition of a former owner has reportedly been seen with moving plates, unexplained voices and sudden chills in this historic restaurant. This historic Fenland hotel is linked to one of the county's more unusual ghost stories. Reports suggest the building is haunted by a ghostly black dog, while local folklore has helped cement its reputation as one of the eeriest places in Cambridgeshire. Reports suggest The Cross Keys in Chatteris is haunted by a ghostly black dog. (Image: Google Maps/Street View) Formerly known as The New Inn, The Coach House is linked to tales of a mysterious "Tall Man" thought by some to be the ghost of the Earl of Holland. Sightings have reportedly been made over the years. The 400-year-old Angel Inn is said to be haunted by the ghost of a former chef. According to local stories, staff and customers have experienced strange noises and sightings over the years. He is believed to be a friendly presence, but there are no details about who he was or how and when he died. The Coach House in St Neots is linked to tales of a mysterious "Tall Man" thought by some to be the ghost of the Earl of Holland. (Image: Google Maps/Street View) Another Cambridgeshire pub, The White Hart in Godmanchester, is linked to historical reports of poltergeist activity, including ashtrays and furniture being moved after closing time.

metadata.title: Binman tells all UK households to make food bin change urgently
metadata.contentSnippet: A bin collector has urged UK households to mark food waste caddies with their house number to prevent them blowing away in autumn winds.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Binman tells all UK households to make food bin change urgently
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Households risk losing food waste caddies in autumn winds unless lids are clearly numbered. A refuse collector has urged residents across the UK to mark outdoor containers now before seasonal autumn gales arrive in force. Ashley, known on TikTok as The No1 Binman to his 214,600 followers, shared the advice as temperatures drop across the country. He said: "It's that time of year where the wind starts picking up and if you have a food waste bin and don't have your number on it, it could end up a million miles down the road." Householders often blame council collection crews when kerbside bins vanish, but collectors explain that empty food caddies weigh very little once emptied into lorries on collection rounds. Ashley said: "It's not the bin men's fault, it's because they don't weigh a lot." "So once you take the food out, they get put down and if they're not taken in straight away, they could end up down the road." Numbers marked clearly on the top lid allow waste collection crews to return containers directly outside the correct property after emptying. Ashley pointed out that identification stickers can be applied to food waste containers and standard general rubbish wheelie bins alike. He added: "The bin men will make sure it goes right back outside your house and then it's up to you to go and get it." The bin worker previously shared advice on marking bin lids to prevent bins from wandering across streets on collection day. In addition to outdoor containers, guidance outlines steps to maintain hygiene in kitchen caddies as central heating turns on. Kitchen containers should be emptied every two to three days during autumn to stop dampness, fruit flies and odours from developing. Caddies should always be lined with official council-approved compostable or biodegradable liners to keep bins clean and stop liquids from leaking. Hot scraps such as soup or leftover portions must also be allowed to cool completely before disposal, preventing condensation from building up inside the caddy. Households should tie a tight knot in compostable liners before dropping them into outdoor kerbside bins to keep larger containers clean. Retrieving emptied caddies as quickly as possible on collection mornings ensures containers will not blow away down the street.

metadata.title: East Anglian Book Awards 2026 shortlist announced

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: East Anglian Book Awards 2026 shortlist announced
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The shortlisted titles for the East Anglian Book Awards 2026, the East of England’s leading celebration of writing and publishing talent, have been announced today, alongside the shortlist for the City of Literature Award. Now in their 19th year, the awards are presented by the National Centre for Writing, in partnership with the Eastern Daily Press and Norwich UNESCO City of Literature, with support from UEA’s faculty of arts and humanities. This year's shortlist includes a memoir, described by Vogue as "genuinely jaw dropping", exploring fame, mental illness and wellness culture; a lyrical children's picture book about love and loss; and a celebration of 100 years of the Norfolk Wildlife Trust. The selected writers all have strong connections to Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Essex, Hertfordshire, Norfolk or Suffolk, with many living and working in the region today. Paula Sanchez, chief executive and creative director of the National Centre for Writing, says: "Year on year, we are delighted to see growing interest in the East Anglian Book Awards, alongside increasing support from writers, publishers, booksellers, libraries and readers across the region. "The east of England has a remarkable literary culture. From its distinctive landscapes and rich storytelling heritage to its thriving independent publishers, festivals and writing communities, it is one of the UK's most vibrant homes for literature. This year's shortlist reflects the extraordinary breadth of writing being produced by authors with roots in the region, from fiction and poetry to history, memoir and children's books. I can't wait to discover these books and celebrate the writers behind them." East Anglian Book Awards 2026 shortlist Fiction ·       Family Friends by Chloe Ashby (Fig Tree) ·       About to Fall Apart by Ashley Hickson-Lovence (Faber) ·       Almost Life by Kiran Millwood Hargrave (Picador) Poetry ·       55 Devotionals (Against Erasure) by Andrew McDonnell (Broken Sleep Books) ·       A Place to Get Better by Imogen McHugh (Erbacce Press) ·       Later Life Letter by Luke Wright (Little, Brown) History and Tradition ·       The Path More Travelled: The Secret History of Britain's Footpaths by Nicholas Crane (Orion) ·       The Archaeology of Norfolk's First World War Airfields by Gary Rossin (Poppyland Publishing) ·       The Dark Black Days of War: The Great War Diary of Honor Elwes by Juliet Webster (Poppyland Publishing) Biography and Memoir ·       The Make-Believe by Hannah Murray (Hutchinson Heinemann) ·       Andrew Dodds Reporting by Elly Robinson (Jardine Press) ·       John Henry Gurney: A Passion for Birds by C. A. Slater, P. J. Mundy, and R. B. Williams (John Beaufoy Publishing) General Non-Fiction ·       This Wild Dream by Nick Acheson (Propolis) ·       Wetland Wings: The History of Holkham Marsh and its Birds by Andrew Bloomfield (Holkham Estate) ·       Thoughtlands: Walking in Writers' Suffolk by Jacky Colliss Harvey (Haus Publishing) Children’s Books ·       Project Human by Pen Avey (UpLit Press) ·       Tiger's Last Roar by Harriet Howe (Bonnier Books) ·       The Wood Where Stories Sing by Andy Shepherd (Bonnier Books) Debut Novels ·       Venus, Vanishing by Rebecca Birrell (Picador) ·       The Leveret by Anna Goldreich (Hamish Hamilton) ·       Prairie Oyster by Sophie Robinson (Little, Brown) Among the shortlisted writers is Hannah Murray, Game of Thrones actress turned published author. Her memoir, The Make-Believe, has been shortlisted in the Biography and Memoir category. Hannah Murray (Image: Sophie Davidson) Hannah said: "I'm ecstatic to be shortlisted. East Anglia is where I feel I truly became a writer, where much of The Make-Believe was written and shaped, and where I have found the most wonderful literary community. This region inspires and fosters so much incredible writing and I'm really proud to call it home." Also shortlisted is Suffolk-based writer Luke Wright, who has been writing and performing poetry for nearly 20 years. His latest title, Later Life Letter, has been nominated in the Poetry category. Luke Wright (Image: Emily Fae) He said: "I’m delighted to have been shortlisted for an East Anglian Book Award. Later Life Letter is in many ways the story of my life and so much of that life has unfolded here in East Anglia, in Coggeshall, Norwich and for the last 16 years in Bungay. "We have so many brilliant poets and writers in the east of England, so it’s particularly lovely to have this very personal book recognised on home turf." Category winners will be announced in the Eastern Daily Press and other Newsquest titles in January, followed by the Overall Book of the Year and City of Literature Awards, presented at a special event at the National Centre for Writing in Norwich on Thursday February 11. Tickets are on sale now. City of Literature Award 2026 Also announced is the shortlist for the City of Literature Award, supported by Norwich UNESCO City of Literature. Now in its second year, this award honours individuals and organisations making an outstanding contribution to the region’s literary life through community engagement, publishing innovation or literary advocacy. The nominees are: ·       Good Shout, the longest running poetry open mic in Peterborough, providing performance opportunities to local poets. ·       Heidi Williamson, poet and Writing for Life Fellow for the Royal Literary Fund, running community reading and writing sessions. ·       Rebecca Stonehill, author and founder of Norwich Writers Rebel, a collective of writers who are engaging with the climate and nature emergency in their work. ·       Rhyme Against the Machine, a welcoming, playful community which hosts poetry open mic nights at Dead Wax in Norwich. ·       Tamar Yoseloff, award-winning poet and teacher. The winner of the City of Literature Award 2026 will be decided by public vote. To qualify for this year’s awards, works must be set predominantly in Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Essex, Hertfordshire, Norfolk or Suffolk, or authored by someone living in the region. Books must have been published for the first time between August 6 2025 and August 5 2026. They must have been commercially available in physical bookshops. For full details and to find out how to vote for the City of Literature Award 2026, visit the National Centre for Writing website: nationalcentreforwriting.org.uk/eaba. Since its inception, the East Anglian Book Awards have honoured more than 150 authors, 200 titles and 100 publishers. Past winners include The Meaning of Geese by Nick Acheson, Iron Man by Lynne Bryan, The House of One Hundred Clocks by A.M. Howell, and After Me Comes The Flood by Sarah Perry, who later won the Baileys Women’s Prize for Fiction.

events.title: 5 long lost railway stations in Cambridgeshire you may not have heard of
events.content: Cambridgeshire's railway network was once far larger than it is today, with long-lost stations serving market towns, villages and growing industrial centres across the county. While many have since disappeared, their stories remain woven into the landscape, offering fascinating reminders of a very different age of travel. Before Peterborough became synonymous with the East Coast Main Line, the city's first railway station was Peterborough East. Opened in 1845 by the Eastern Counties Railway, it served routes towards Northampton, Rugby, March, Wisbech and Norwich. The station was known simply as Peterborough until being renamed Peterborough East in 1923. Passenger services ended in June 1966 as part of wider railway cutbacks, although the site continued handling parcels traffic until 1970. Today, little remains apart from the historic engine sheds, but the former station played a crucial role in shaping Peterborough's growth into a major railway city. metadata.title: Only one in five people can pass this three-question IQ test
metadata.contentSnippet: The Cognitive Reflection Test has a pass rate of just 17 per cent, leaving the majority who attempt it boggled.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Only one in five people can pass this three-question IQ test
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Less than one in five people pass this IQ test, thought to be the shortest in the world only three questions long. The Cognitive Reflection Test has a pass rate of just 17 per cent, leaving the majority who attempt it boggled. It was originally part of a research paper published in 2005 by MIT Professor Shane Frederick, and has recently resurfaced online with many people giving it a go. As part of his research, Professor Frederick had more than 3,000 participants from a range of educational backgrounds complete the test, but even those attending top American universities such as Yale and Harvard struggled to work out all the answers. Professor Frederick said: "The three items on the CRT are ‘easy’ in the sense that their solution is easily understood when explained, yet reaching the correct answer often requires the suppression of an erroneous answer that springs ‘impulsively’ to mind." So how will you get on? 1. A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost? 2. If it takes five machines five minutes to make five widgets, how long would it take 100 machines to make 100 widgets? 3. In a lake, there is a patch of lily pads. Every day, the patch doubles in size. If it takes 48 days for the patch to cover the entire lake, how long would it take for the patch to cover half of the lake? These are the three most common answers that people guess, but they are actually incorrect: 1. 10 cents 2. 100 minutes 3. 24 days Professor Frederick said: "Anyone who reflects upon it for even a moment would recognise that the difference between $1 and 10 cents is only 90 cents, not $1 as the problem stipulates. "In this case, catching that error is tantamount to solving the problem, since nearly everyone who does not respond ‘10 cents’ does, in fact, give the correct response." The correct answers are: 1. Five cents 2. Five minutes 3. 47 days Presh Talwalkar, the author of The Hoy of Game Theory: An Introduction to Strategic Thinking, explained how to work out the correct answers for each of the three questions on his blog, Mind Your Decisions. 1. Say the ball costs X. Then the bat costs $1 more, so it is X + 1. So we have bat + ball = X + (X + 1) = 1.1 because together they cost $1.10. This means 2X + 1 = 1.1, then 2X = 0.1, so X = 0.05. This means the ball costs five cents and the bat costs $1.05 2. If it takes five machines five minutes to make five widgets, then it takes one machine five minutes to make one widget (each machine is making a widget in five minutes). If we have 100 machines working together, then each can make a widget in five minutes. So there will be 100 widgets in five minutes. 3. Every day FORWARD the patch doubles in size. So every day BACKWARDS means the patch halves in size. So on day 47 the lake is half full.

metadata.title: Does home insurance cover storm damage? What homeowners need to know
metadata.contentSnippet: Find out whether home insurance policies cover wind damage to properties, fences, sheds, gates and other outdoor items.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Does home insurance cover storm damage? What homeowners need to know
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Stormy weather can leave homeowners facing unexpected repair bills, particularly when strong winds damage roofs, fences and other parts of a property. While home insurance can provide protection against some types of storm damage, not everything is necessarily covered. The exact level of protection will depend on your policy and what has been damaged. Here’s what homeowners should know before making a claim. Storm Boelo will bring wet and windy weather across the UK this weekend 🍃🌧️ Here are the details to help you make your plans 👇 https://t.co/Yx3CYaUr3I — Met Office (@metoffice) October 23, 2026 Buildings and contents insurance policies often cover against storm damage. Following a storm, your policy should cover any significant damage that your house suffers as a result of high winds from the storm. However, policies often exclude anything outdoors, such as garden furniture, garden sheds, fences, gates or hedges, so specific cover would need to be found for them. Matthew Harwood, Home & Lifestyle insurance expert at Confused.com , said: "Having home insurance in place helps protect your building and contents from potential storm damage, particularly if you live in an area at high risk of flooding. "It's also important to buy home insurance if your home has features like a thatched roof, timber frames or is made of wattle and daub. These kinds of homes are typically made from old-fashioned construction methods, which makes them more likely to suffer storm damage. "It's also worth checking how much home insurance cover you need to avoid missing key features that help cover your home from storm damage." With high winds still prevalent across much of the UK, many garden fences will be looking a little worse for wear, and may even have blown away. However, fences aren’t normally covered for storm damage under standard home insurance policies, but it would still be worth checking your specific insurance policy to make sure. As wear and tear is rarely covered by most insurers, any fences that were already old and unstable prior to a storm will likely not be covered by your police. You may end up having to prove to your insurer that your fence was well-maintained prior to the high winds which caused the damage.

metadata.title: 'Career burglar' who stole war service medal and training sword jailed again
metadata.contentSnippet: A career burglar has been jailed again after stealing a martial arts training sword and a Great War service medal in Peterborough.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Career burglar' who stole war service medal and training sword jailed again
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A serial burglar has been jailed again after stealing a martial arts training sword and a Great War service medal. Jody Stones, 41, was released from prison in May 2025 but carried out more burglaries in Peterborough this year. On July 28, 2026, he broke into a property in Rivendale, Werrington, and stole a gilet and a martial arts training sword worth about £740. A blood smear on a kitchen cupboard door matched Stones, while CCTV showed him outside with the stolen sword. Two weeks later, Stones and another masked man broke into a home on Eastfield Road while the elderly resident was inside. The victim woke to find Stones standing by his bed. When challenged, Stones jumped from a first-floor balcony and fled with the victim’s wallet, bank cards, passport, cufflinks, coin and stamp collection, gold watch and grandfather’s Great War service medal. CCTV showed one of the men wearing the same clothes as Stones during the Rivendale burglary. Enquiries showed Stones had approached local collectibles dealers to sell the stolen coins. Officers recovered the stolen coins and his grandfather’s medal and returned them to the victim. Stones was arrested on August 17 when he went to Thorpe Wood Police Station to answer bail for an unrelated matter. He pleaded guilty to two burglaries and was jailed for six years and nine months at Peterborough Crown Court on October 16. He also admitted six more burglaries, three car thefts and handling stolen goods. The other man seen on CCTV with Stones has yet to be identified. Detective Constable George Corney said: "Stones is a career burglar who showed a complete disregard for the sentence he was already serving for the exact same offences. “He stole not only valuable items, but items of real sentimental value to the victims and even burgled one address while the homeowner was asleep. "I can only imagine how terrifying it must have been for him to wake up and find a masked man beside his bed. "I am glad Stones is now back behind bars."

Ibrahim Doğuş, Founder of the British Kebab Awards, said: "Reaching the final is a significant achievement, and this year’s finalists reflect the talent and hard work of the whole industry — from independent family businesses to larger restaurant groups." So without further ado, here are all the Cambridgeshire finalists in the 2027 British Kebab Awards. Cambourne Grill Kebab is a finalist for Kebab Van of the Year. Burwell Kebab Van is a finalist for Kebab Van of the Year. Hungry Kebab is a finalist for Kebab Van of the Year. Diamond Kebab is a finalist for Kebab Van of the Year. Grilla Soham is a finalist for Kebab Van of the Year. Public voting continues for all finalists until 31 January 2027, and the independent judging panel will reconvene in the first week of February to determine the winners in each category. Mr Doğuş added: "More than 6,000 nominations and over 40,000 votes show how strongly people support these businesses. metadata.title: Cambridge Film Festival's 45th edition to feature Palme d’Or winner and premieres
metadata.contentSnippet: Major award winners and standout new talent will headline this year’s Cambridge Film Festival.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridge Film Festival's 45th edition to feature Palme d’Or winner and premieres
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Major award winners and standout new talent will headline this year’s Cambridge Film Festival. Returning for its 45th edition, the festival runs until November 1 at the Cambridge Arts Picturehouse, and will feature 11 days of international cinema, UK and European premieres, documentaries, short films, and family favourites. Among the highlights are gala screenings of Clio Barnard’s I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner Fjord, and Jesse Eisenberg’s latest feature The Debut. The programme spans major Cannes prizewinners, hotly anticipated new releases, and films from emerging voices in contemporary cinema. Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine will close the festival. Savina Petkova, programming lead, said: "We’re two weeks away from opening the doors on our 45th Festival, and what excites me most is the sheer breadth of the programme. "We have the Palme d’Or winner, Cannes prizewinners, films that are already gathering serious awards attention and brilliant new voices that audiences may be discovering for the first time. "But Cambridge Film Festival has never been about chasing prestige for its own sake. "It’s about putting great films in front of curious audiences and creating the chance to discover something unexpected. "You can come for Fjord or Fatherland, stay for a documentary about doctors working in Gaza, catch Bend It Like Beckham with the family, and end the night with a film you’ve never heard of before. "That’s the joy of a festival." The festival also features an Environment & Community strand, a Family Film Festival with free screenings, and BFI's Rip It Up: Out Loud, which explores youth rebellion and self-expression through cinema. In addition to screenings, the festival will host an industry day, film quiz, audience and jury awards, and a special 45th-anniversary screening of Portrait of a Lady on Fire.

metadata.contentSnippet: A fire at Roman Court in Leverington near Wisbech, which is earmarked for asylum seeker accommodation, is being treated as arson.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Fire at proposed asylum seeker site being treated as arson
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A fire at a site earmarked for asylum seeker accommodation in Cambridgeshire is being treated as arson. Firefighters were called to the blaze at Roman Court, Leverington, near Wisbech, at 7.26pm on Wednesday (October 21). The fire service called police to the scene at 7.37pm. Crews from Wisbech, March and Dogsthorpe, along with the turntable ladder from Stanground rushed to the scene. Appliances from Outwell and West Walton, in Norfolk, also attended the incident, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service confirmed. A Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service spokesperson said: "Firefighters arrived to find a fire in a single storey building that was unoccupied. Emergency services rushed to a single-storey building fire at Roman Court (Image: Colin Martin) "They are working hard to tackle the fire and prevent it from spreading. There are currently no injuries reported. "An investigation will be carried out to establish the cause of the fire once it is fully extinguished." Police confirmed on Thursday, October 22, that the fire was being treated as arson and was under investigation. No injuries were reported but the building has been "severely damaged", police said. Anyone with information should contact police online at www.cambs.police.uk/report quoting incident 452 of 21 October. Anyone without internet access should call 101.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A burglar who broke into a Cambridge burger restaurant and stole more than £900 has been jailed. Robert Rust, 39, of Howard Road, Cambridge, broke into 5 Akhis on Chesterton Road on October 10, smashing the glass front door and stealing a till containing £918.75 in cash. He was also linked to eight shop thefts from Tesco in Chesterton and Co-op in Milton Avenue between October 2 and 12. In addition, Rust was identified as the thief behind three bike thefts between September 21 and October 4 from Milton Road, Station Square, and Sidney Street. At Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on October 20, he pleaded guilty to burglary, using threatening behaviour to cause alarm/distress, three counts of bike theft, and eight counts of shop theft. He was sentenced to nine months in prison. PC Luke Upcott, from the Spree Offender Team, said: “Rust targeted local businesses and members of the public over a matter of weeks, showing a clear disregard for the impact his crimes had on others. “We are committed to identifying prolific offenders and bringing them before the courts.”
